lessons.title: The Gemini model lineup and how to choose
lessons.summary: Know the model families, what each is for, and how to pick the cheapest model that passes your evals.

sections.heading: The families you will actually use
sections.body:
At the time of writing (November 2026), the Gemini API groups models roughly like this. Model ids change often, so always confirm them on the models page before shipping.

- **Gemini 4 Argon** (`gemini-4-argon`): Google's flagship reasoning model for hard coding, agentic, maths and science work. Its 1,048,576-token context window is shared by input, thinking and output.
- **Flash models** (for example `gemini-3.8-flash`, the most capable Flash at the time of writing): fast and much cheaper. They are the default for most production apps and agents.
- **Flash-Lite models** (for example `gemini-3.5-flash-lite`): the fastest and cheapest, for high-throughput classification, routing and extraction.
- **What about "Pro"?** Older material talks about Pro, Flash and Flash-Lite. At the time of writing there is no stable Pro model: the only Pro is a preview (`gemini-3.1-pro-preview`), and `gemini-2.5-pro` is deprecated. The flagship tier is now Gemini 4 Argon. Note that Argon and the Pro preview are not on the Free tier, while the current Flash and Flash-Lite models are.
- **Specialised models**: for example Live models for real-time voice, text-to-speech models, image- and music-generation models (such as Lyria for music), and Gemini embedding models (`gemini-embedding-2`, `gemini-embedding-001`) for search and RAG. Check the models page for the current ids.
- **Gemma**: Google's open-weight models, which you download and run yourself (on your own hardware or through Model Garden on Google Cloud). They are not served by the Gemini API model list in the same way.

sections.heading: A selection method that survives model churn
sections.body:
1. Write a small eval set: 20–50 real inputs with expected outputs or grading rules.
2. Start with a Flash or Flash-Lite model. Measure quality, latency and cost.
3. Move up to a bigger model only for the cases that fail, or route by difficulty: Flash-Lite classifies the request, Flash handles most of it, and Argon takes the hard ones.
4. Re-run the eval whenever you change model, prompt or thinking level.

The capability, latency and cost triangle never goes away. The right answer is the cheapest model that meets your quality bar *on your own evals*, not the top of a public leaderboard.

sections.heading: Aliases, previews and deprecations
sections.body:
The models page describes four version patterns:

- **Stable** (like `gemini-3.6-flash` or `gemini-3.5-flash-lite`): usually doesn't change. Most production apps should pin one.
- **Preview** (ending in `-preview`): may be used for production and is typically billed, but can have more restrictive rate limits and can be deprecated with as little as about two weeks' notice. Treat it as something you can lose quickly.
- **Latest** aliases (such as `gemini-flash-latest`): hot-swapped to each new release, with an email notice shortly before. Convenient for prototypes, but behaviour changes under you without a code change.
- **Experimental**: not for production.

**Deprecation** means support has ended and a shutdown is announced; **shutdown** means the endpoint is gone. Published shutdown dates are the *earliest possible* dates. In 2026 a new pattern appeared: **automatic routing**, where a deprecated stable id keeps working but is served by a successor model and billed at the successor's rates. For example, the docs say that from 1 December 2026 `gemini-2.5-flash` routes to `gemini-3.5-flash-lite` and `gemini-2.5-pro` routes to `gemini-3.8-flash`.

Routing keeps your code running, but it is still a model change: outputs, latency and cost can all shift. Track the deprecations page, run your eval set against the successor before the date, and migrate deliberately.

keyPoints: Flash is the default workhorse; Flash-Lite for volume; Argon for the hardest reasoning and agentic work.
Pin stable model ids in production; previews and `-latest` aliases can change behaviour without a code change.
Choose models with your own eval set, not a leaderboard.
Gemma is open-weight: you host it, the Gemini API does not.
A deprecated id that is auto-routed still works, but it is served (and billed) as a different model, so re-run your evals.

gotchas.trap: Defaulting every request to the flagship model "to be safe".
gotchas.correct: Start with Flash or Flash-Lite, measure on evals, and route only the hard cases to Argon.

gotchas.trap: Shipping a `-preview` model id or a `-latest` alias in production.
gotchas.correct: Pin a stable id and migrate deliberately, re-running your eval set.

gotchas.trap: Assuming automatic routing of a deprecated model means "nothing to do".
gotchas.correct: Routing swaps in a different model with different behaviour and pricing. Evaluate the successor and migrate on your own schedule.

lessons.lab: Create a free API key in Google AI Studio. Write 10 test prompts for a task you care about (for example classifying support tickets). Run them on a Flash-Lite, a Flash and the Argon model, and record quality, latency and token usage in a small table. Decide which model you'd ship and why.

lessons.title: Calling Gemini: the Interactions API
lessons.summary: The Interactions API is the recommended interface for new projects. Learn requests, steps, server-side state and stateless mode.

sections.heading: Your first call
Interactions and steps
sections.body:
An **interaction** is one complete turn in a conversation or task. Instead of role-tagged messages, it holds a chronological list of typed **steps**: `user_input`, `thought`, `function_call`, `function_result`, server-tool steps such as `google_search_call` and `google_search_result`, and the final `model_output`. Steps make debugging and UI rendering easier, because you can see exactly what happened.

- `output_text` is a convenience property that gives you the final text.
- `interactions.create` returns the model-generated steps. `interactions.get` also includes the `user_input` steps.
- When the model asks for a function, you reply with a `function_result` step that carries the matching `call_id`.
- Managed agents use the same endpoint: you pass `agent=` instead of `model=`.

sections.heading: Server-side state with previous_interaction_id
sections.body:
By default (`store=True`) the server keeps the interaction, so you can continue a conversation without resending history:

```python
turn1 = client.interactions.create(model="gemini-3.8-flash", input="Hi, my name is Priya.")
turn2 = client.interactions.create(
    model="gemini-3.8-flash",
    input="What is my name?",
    previous_interaction_id=turn1.id,
)
```

Two things catch people out:

- **Only the conversation carries over.** `tools`, `system_instruction` and `generation_config` are interaction-scoped, so you must send them again on every turn.
- **Retention is limited.** At the time of writing, stored interactions are kept for 55 days on the paid tier (configurable to shorter periods) and 1 day on the free tier. You can also delete a stored interaction explicitly.

sections.heading: Stateless mode
sections.body: Set `store=False` if you must not keep data on the server. Then you send the full history yourself on every request, including the model's previous `thought` and `function_call` steps exactly as received (thoughts carry signatures the model needs). Stateless mode can't use `previous_interaction_id`, and combining `store=False` with `background=True` is rejected with a 400 error, because background execution needs a stored interaction to poll.

sections.heading: The legacy generateContent API and migrating from it
sections.body:
`generateContent` (`client.models.generate_content(...)`) is the older API. It is called legacy but "remains fully supported"; the Interactions API is the default for new work. You still meet it in three places:

- **Existing code** written before the Interactions API became the default.
- **Features not yet in Interactions**: the Batch API, explicit context caching (on supported older models; not on Gemini 4 Argon or later), and automatic function calling in the Python SDK.
- **Older samples and tutorials**.

The migration guide maps the concepts roughly like this:

| generateContent | Interactions API |
|---|---|
| `contents` | `input` |
| `candidates` / `parts` | `steps` / `output_text` |
| output settings such as JSON mode | top-level `response_format` |
| `generate_content_stream` | `interactions.create(stream=True)` |
| `functionResponse` part | `function_result` step with `call_id` |

Two Gemini 3+ rules bite people who keep using generateContent: a `FunctionResponse` must include the `call_id` and `name` of the call it answers, and a request that ends in a **prefilled model turn** (a partial assistant answer for the model to continue) returns a 400 error. `candidate_count` is also unsupported on Gemini 3+.

keyPoints: Interactions API = recommended for new projects; `generateContent` = legacy but supported.
`previous_interaction_id` keeps history server-side; tools, system instruction and generation config must be resent each turn.
`store=False` means stateless: resend full history, no background mode.
Read `output_text` for the answer and `steps` to see thoughts, tool calls and results.
You still meet `generateContent` for the Batch API, explicit caching on older models, Python automatic function calling and existing code.
Migration: `contents` becomes `input`; `candidates`/`parts` become `steps`/`output_text`; function responses become `function_result` steps with a `call_id`.

gotchas.trap: Assuming the system instruction and tools persist when you pass `previous_interaction_id`.
gotchas.correct: Resend `tools`, `system_instruction` and `generation_config` on every turn; only the conversation history is carried.

gotchas.trap: Turning on `store=False` for privacy and then trying to use background execution.
gotchas.correct: Background execution needs storage. Use stateless mode only for normal synchronous calls.

gotchas.trap: Porting an old prompt that ends with a prefilled model turn ("Sure, here is the JSON: {") to a Gemini 3+ model.
gotchas.correct: Prefilled final model turns return 400 on Gemini 3+. Ask for the format in the instructions or use `response_format` instead.

lessons.lab: Build a 3-turn CLI chat with `previous_interaction_id` and a system instruction ("You are a terse travel assistant"). Then remove the system instruction from turns 2 and 3 and watch the tone drift. Finally, re-implement it in stateless mode with `store=False` and send the full history yourself.

lessons.title: Prompting Gemini well, and thinking levels
lessons.summary: System instructions, clear task specs, examples, and how to set thinking levels (and why sampling parameters no longer matter) on current Gemini models.

sections.heading: A prompt that works
sections.body:
Good Gemini prompts read like a precise brief to a capable colleague:

- **Be precise and direct.** State the task, the audience, the length and format, and what to do when information is missing. Define any term that could be read two ways.
- **System instruction for stable things.** Persona, constraints and output format go in the system instruction (or at the very beginning of the user prompt). Per-request data goes in `input`.
- **Consistent delimiters.** Label the parts of the prompt with XML-style tags *or* Markdown headings, and use one style throughout so instructions, documents and examples do not blur together.
- **Few-shot examples.** The docs recommend including examples, formatted consistently with each other and with the output you want.
- **Ask for detail when you want it.** Gemini 3-generation models are concise by default, so request verbosity explicitly.
- **Long context: content first, question last.** Supply all the context first and put your specific instruction at the very end, anchored with a phrase such as "Based on the information above...".
- **No need to ask for visible reasoning.** Thinking models already reason internally; "show your steps" is generally unnecessary.

sections.heading: Thinking levels
sections.body:
Current Gemini models reason before answering. You set the effort with `thinking_level` in `generation_config`: `minimal`, `low`, `medium` or `high`. **Supported levels and defaults differ by model:**

| Model | Levels | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Gemini 4 Argon | low / medium / high | medium |
| Gemini 3.8 Flash | low / medium / high (`minimal` returns an error) | medium |
| Gemini 3.6 Flash | minimal / low / medium / high | medium |
| Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite | minimal / low / medium / high | minimal |

```python
interaction = client.interactions.create(
    model="gemini-4-argon",
    input="Find the race condition in this retry loop and rewrite it safely: ...",
    generation_config={"thinking_level": "medium", "thinking_summaries": "auto"},
)
print(interaction.usage.total_thought_tokens)
```

- `minimal` means the model *likely* will not think, but it still can. Thinking cannot be fully switched off on 4 Argon or the Gemini 3 Flash / Flash-Lite models.
- Higher levels cost more tokens and take longer, so evaluate your workload at several levels and use the lowest one that meets your quality bar.
- `max_output_tokens` is a hard cap on **thinking plus output combined**. If the model hits it while reasoning you get `MAX_TOKENS` and a truncated or empty answer, and the thinking is still billed. Prefer lowering `thinking_level` to shrinking the cap; for 4 Argon the docs say to use at least 32,768.
- Thinking tokens are billed at the output rate and reported in `usage.total_thought_tokens`.
- **Thought summaries:** by default only the final output is returned. Set `thinking_summaries: "auto"` to get a summary. You still pay for the full thoughts, not just the summary.
- **Legacy `thinking_budget`** (the 2.5-series control) is deprecated on 4 Argon: sent alone it is mapped to the nearest level with a warning, but sending **both** `thinking_budget` and `thinking_level` returns **400**. Do not combine them on 3.x models either.

sections.heading: Sampling parameters on the newest models
sections.body: Older models let you tune `temperature`, `top_p` and `top_k`. Starting with Gemini 3.6 Flash and 3.5 Flash-Lite, and on Gemini 4 Argon and all later releases, these parameters are **ignored**, and Google warns they will cause errors in future generations. Remove them during migration instead of tuning them. Control quality and consistency with the prompt, few-shot examples, the thinking level, structured output for fixed formats, and evals.

keyPoints: Persona, constraints and output format go in the system instruction; per-request data goes in the input.
Use one delimiter style, define ambiguous terms, include consistent few-shot examples, and ask explicitly for verbosity.
`thinking_level` is the reasoning control; supported levels differ by model (`minimal` errors on 3.8 Flash and 4 Argon).
`max_output_tokens` covers thinking + output; lower the thinking level rather than starving the cap.
Thinking tokens are billed as output, even when you only see a summary.
Sampling parameters are ignored on 3.6 Flash, 3.5 Flash-Lite, 4 Argon and later: remove them.
Never send `thinking_budget` and `thinking_level` together (400 on 4 Argon).

gotchas.trap: Setting `max_output_tokens: 1024` on a hard reasoning task and getting empty or cut-off answers.
gotchas.correct: Thinking shares the cap. Raise `max_output_tokens` (at least 32,768 on Argon) or lower the thinking level.

gotchas.trap: Lowering temperature on Gemini 4 Argon to make it more deterministic.
gotchas.correct: Current models ignore sampling parameters. Tighten the prompt, add examples, and use structured output for fixed formats.

gotchas.trap: Setting `thinking_level: "minimal"` on Gemini 3.8 Flash to cut latency.
gotchas.correct: 3.8 Flash supports low/medium/high only; `minimal` returns an error. Use `low`, or a model that supports `minimal` such as 3.5 Flash-Lite.

gotchas.trap: Keeping an old `thinking_budget` and adding `thinking_level` during a migration to Argon.
gotchas.correct: Sending both returns 400. Remove `thinking_budget` and use `thinking_level` only.

lessons.lab: Take one hard prompt (a tricky bug or a logic puzzle). Run it on Argon at `low`, `medium` and `high`, recording answer quality, latency and `usage.total_thought_tokens`. Turn on `thinking_summaries: "auto"` and compare the thought tokens with and without it. Then set `max_output_tokens` to 2,000 at `high` and observe what happens. Finally try `minimal` on 3.8 Flash and on 3.5 Flash-Lite and note the difference.

lessons.title: Multimodal input and the Files API
lessons.summary: Send images, audio, video and PDFs to Gemini, choose between inline data, the Files API, Cloud Storage and URLs, control media tokens, and prompt well with media.

sections.heading: Multimodal by default
sections.body:
Gemini models accept text, images, audio, video and documents such as PDFs in the same request. Each part is a typed content block with a source:

```python
myfile = client.files.upload(file="lecture-03.mp3")

interaction = client.interactions.create(
    model="gemini-3.8-flash",
    input=[
        {"type": "audio", "uri": myfile.uri, "mime_type": myfile.mime_type},
        {"type": "text", "text": "Summarise this lecture by topic with timestamps."},
    ],
)
```

Block types include `image`, `audio`, `video` and `document`. Typical uses: OCR and document understanding, chart reading, meeting and lecture summaries, video Q&A with timestamps, and screenshot debugging. Office formats are being added over time; at the time of writing some (such as DOC and PPT) are rendered as page images.

sections.heading: Choosing an input method
sections.body:
| Method | Limit (at the time of writing) | Persistence | Use when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Inline data | 100 MB per request (50 MB for PDFs) | None | Small, one-off media |
| Files API | 2 GB per file, 20 GB per project | 48 hours | Request over 100 MB, or the same media reused across requests |
| Cloud Storage (GCS) URI registration | 2 GB per file | Access for up to 30 days | Media already lives in a bucket |
| External URL | 15 MB per file | None | Small public files |

- The Files API is free of charge. Uploaded files are deleted automatically after 48 hours; you can delete them sooner.
- You can't download files you uploaded, only see their metadata. Model-generated files can be downloaded.
- Keep your own source of truth (for example a bucket) and re-upload when a file expires.

sections.heading: Media tokens and resolution
sections.body:
Media is billed as input tokens. On Gemini 3 and 4 you can set a per-item `resolution` (media resolution) to trade detail for tokens:

| Setting | Image | Video (per frame) | PDF (per page) |
|---|---|---|---|
| default | 1120 | 70 | 560 |
| `low` | 280 | 70 | 280 |
| `medium` | 560 | 70 | 560 |
| `high` | 1120 | 280 | 1120 |

Recommended starting points: images `high`; PDFs `medium` (quality saturates there, so `high` mostly adds cost); video `low` or `medium` (they are treated the same), or `high` only when frames contain small text you must read. Audio is a flat 25 tokens per second.

Video is sampled statically at 1 frame per second by default. For long videos, **agentic video understanding** (`processing: "agentic"` on the video block in the Interactions API) lets the model choose what to look at, which Google says can cut input cost by up to 88%. It is supported on 4 Argon, 3.8 Flash, 3.6 Flash and 3.5 Flash-Lite.

Check the cost before or after a call: `client.models.count_tokens(...)` up front, or `interaction.usage` (`total_input_tokens`, `total_thought_tokens`, and so on) afterwards.

sections.heading: Prompting with media
sections.body:
- Put the media first and the question after it, just as with long documents.
- Ask for **timestamps** or **page numbers** so answers can be checked.
- For very long videos, ask for a chapter outline first, then drill into one chapter at a time.
- Be specific about what to look at ("the table on page 4", "the error dialog in the bottom-right") rather than "describe this".
- Pick the resolution for the job: a dense spreadsheet screenshot needs more detail than a photo you only need to classify.
- Long videos and audio can use a large share of the context window, so check `usage` and budget accordingly.

keyPoints: Text, image, audio, video and documents can be mixed in one request as typed content blocks.
Inline: 100 MB per request (50 MB PDFs). Files API: 2 GB/file, 20 GB/project, 48-hour retention, free. External URLs: 15 MB. GCS registration: up to 30 days of access.
Use the Files API when the request exceeds 100 MB or when the same media is reused.
Per-item media resolution trades detail for tokens: images high, PDFs medium, video low/medium unless frames are text-heavy.
Agentic video processing can sharply cut input cost on long videos.
Media first, question last; ask for timestamps or page numbers so outputs can be verified.

gotchas.trap: Uploading a file once and expecting it to be available next week.
gotchas.correct: Uploaded files expire after 48 hours. Re-upload, or register a Cloud Storage URI (up to 30 days of access).

gotchas.trap: Inlining a 300 MB video in the request body.
gotchas.correct: Inline requests are capped at 100 MB; larger media must go through the Files API (or a registered GCS URI).

gotchas.trap: Setting every PDF page to `high` resolution "to be safe".
gotchas.correct: PDF quality saturates at `medium`; `high` doubles tokens per page for little gain.

gotchas.trap: Passing a 40 MB public file by external URL.
gotchas.correct: External URLs are limited to 15 MB per file at the time of writing. Upload it with the Files API instead.

lessons.lab: Upload a 20-40 minute talk with the Files API. Put the video block before your instruction and ask for a chaptered summary with timestamps, then ask three follow-up questions about specific chapters. Check two timestamps by hand. Repeat once with `processing: "agentic"` and compare `usage.total_input_tokens`. Finally, send a 20-page PDF at `medium` and at `high` resolution and compare tokens and answer quality.

lessons.title: Function calling end to end
lessons.summary: Declare functions, run the call/result loop, pick a tool_choice mode and handle parallel and chained calls.

sections.heading: The loop
sections.body:
Gemini never runs your code. It *asks* you to:

1. You declare functions: a **name**, a **description** and JSON-schema **parameters**.
2. You send the prompt and the declarations.
3. The model returns a `function_call` step with a name, arguments and an id. It does not execute anything.
4. **Your code** validates the arguments and runs the function.
5. You send back a `function_result` step linked by `call_id`.
6. The model uses the result to answer, or asks for another call.

```python
get_order = {
    "type": "function",
    "name": "get_order",
    "description": "Look up an order by its id. Use when the user asks about an order's status or contents.",
    "parameters": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"order_id": {"type": "string", "description": "Order id like A-1234"}},
        "required": ["order_id"],
    },
}

first = client.interactions.create(model="gemini-3.8-flash", input="Where is order A-1234?", tools=[get_order])
call = next(s for s in first.steps if s.type == "function_call")
result = lookup_order(**call.arguments)  # your code, after validating arguments

final = client.interactions.create(
    model="gemini-3.8-flash",
    previous_interaction_id=first.id,
    tools=[get_order],  # resend tools every turn
    input=[{"type": "function_result", "name": call.name, "call_id": call.id,
            "result": [{"type": "text", "text": json.dumps(result)}]}],
)
print(final.output_text)
```

**Things that trip people up in the loop**

- When the model returns a `function_call`, the interaction's status is `requires_action`: it is waiting for your `function_result`.
- `tools`, `system_instruction` and `generation_config` are scoped to one interaction. Resend them on the turn that carries the result.
- `result` is an array of content blocks. On Gemini 3 and later it can hold text and also image, document, audio or video blocks, inline or by `uri`. So a tool can hand back a rendered chart or a PDF, not just a JSON string.
- When streaming, a call's arguments arrive as `arguments_delta` pieces of partial JSON. Concatenate them until the step ends, then parse and validate. Never execute on a partial fragment.
- Automatic function calling (the SDK runs your Python functions for you) is Python-only and works only with the legacy `generateContent` API. In the Interactions API you run the loop yourself.

sections.heading: tool_choice modes
sections.body:
Set `tool_choice` in `generation_config`:

- `auto` (default): the model decides whether to call a function or answer directly.
- `any`: the model is constrained to always predict a function call. Useful to force an action.
- `none`: function calls are prohibited, even though tools are declared. Handy to switch calling off for one turn without editing your tool list.
- `validated`: the model ensures its calls follow your function schema.

To force a call but **limit which functions** are allowed, use the object form:

```python
generation_config={"tool_choice": {"allowed_tools": {"mode": "any", "tools": ["get_order"]}}}
```

**Legacy `generateContent`** uses `function_calling_config.mode` (`AUTO`, `ANY`, `NONE`, `VALIDATED`) plus `allowed_function_names`. `AUTO` is the default when only function declarations are present. `VALIDATED` is the default when built-in tools or structured output are also turned on. It predicts calls or text and enforces the schema, which cuts malformed calls compared with `AUTO`.

sections.heading: Parallel and compositional calls
sections.body:
- **Parallel**: the model can return several independent calls in one turn (for example weather in three cities). Run them, then return **all** the results.
- **Compositional**: calls chained across turns, where one result feeds the next call (look up the forecast, then set the thermostat).
- Keep looping until the model stops asking for calls, with a maximum number of iterations as a safety net.

sections.heading: Designing good tools
sections.body:
- Descriptions are how the model chooses. Say what the tool does, when to use it and when not to.
- Use descriptive names with no spaces or special characters (underscores or camelCase).
- Use strong types, enums and required fields in the schema.
- Keep the active toolset small and non-overlapping. The docs suggest at most 10 to 20 active tools.
- Return concise, meaningful results. On failure, return a clear error message in the result (what went wrong and what to try), not an empty string.
- **Validate arguments in your code before running anything**, and require confirmation for destructive or high-impact actions.

The next lesson covers schema-complexity limits, mixing built-in and custom tools, and the error codes you'll see.

keyPoints: The model returns `function_call` (status `requires_action`); your code runs it and replies with `function_result` matched by `call_id`.
`tool_choice`: auto (default), any (must call), none (no calls), validated (schema adherence). Use `allowed_tools` to limit which functions may be called.
Return all results for parallel calls; loop for compositional calls with an iteration cap.
Aggregate streamed `arguments_delta` before executing; results can be multimodal content blocks.
Always validate arguments before executing; confirm high-impact actions.

gotchas.trap: Expecting Gemini to execute the declared function itself.
gotchas.correct: Gemini only proposes calls. Your application executes them and returns `function_result` steps.

gotchas.trap: Returning only the first result when the model asked for three parallel calls.
gotchas.correct: Run every requested call and return every `function_result`, each with its matching `call_id`.

gotchas.trap: Parsing and running a tool as soon as the first streamed `arguments_delta` arrives.
gotchas.correct: Deltas are partial JSON. Aggregate them until the call step finishes, then parse, validate and execute.

gotchas.trap: Sending the `function_result` turn with `previous_interaction_id` but without `tools`.
gotchas.correct: `tools`, `system_instruction` and `generation_config` are per interaction. Resend them every turn.

lessons.lab: Build a two-tool assistant: `get_weather(city)` and `set_thermostat(celsius)`. Ask "It's cold in Oslo, set my heating sensibly". Log every step, confirm the model chains the calls, and add argument validation that rejects temperatures outside 10–28 °C with a helpful error result.

lessons.title: Structured output with JSON schemas
lessons.summary: Get schema-shaped JSON with response_format, validate it in code, and know which schema keywords are enforced.

sections.heading: Asking for JSON
sections.body:
Set `response_format` with a JSON MIME type and a schema. With Pydantic (Python) or Zod (JavaScript) you define the shape once and validate the result with the same model.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Optional

class Invoice(BaseModel):
    vendor: str = Field(description="Company that issued the invoice")
    invoice_number: str
    total: float
    due_date: Optional[str] = Field(description="ISO date, or null if not printed")

interaction = client.interactions.create(
    model="gemini-3.8-flash",
    input=invoice_text,
    response_format={
        "type": "text",
        "mime_type": "application/json",
        "schema": Invoice.model_json_schema(),
    },
)
invoice = Invoice.model_validate_json(interaction.output_text)
```

sections.heading: What the schema can and can’t enforce
sections.body:
Supported at the time of writing: the basic types (including `null` via a type array such as `["string", "null"]`), `title` and `description`, `properties`, `required`, `additionalProperties`, string `enum` and `format` (date, time, date-time), numeric `enum`/`minimum`/`maximum` (inclusive), array `items`/`prefixItems`/`minItems`/`maxItems`, `anyOf`, and recursive `$ref`/`$defs`.

**Silently ignored**: `minLength`, `maxLength`, `minProperties`, `maxProperties`, `uniqueItems`, `contains`, `minContains` and `maxContains`. They are stripped without an error, so check them in your own code. Note that `minItems`/`maxItems` on arrays **are** enforced.

**Valid is not the same as correct.** The output is guaranteed to be syntactically valid JSON that follows the schema, but the *values* can still be wrong: a total that doesn't match the line items, or a date read from the wrong field. Handle "schema-compliant but semantically incorrect" output with your own checks.

Output follows the key order of your schema. Streamed chunks are valid partial JSON that join into the full object.

Very complex schemas (too many branches, unions or nesting levels) are rejected with `400 INVALID_ARGUMENT`. Simplify them: flatten nesting, reduce unions and trim long enums.

sections.heading: A reliable extraction pattern
sections.body:
1. Schema with **descriptions** on every field and **nullable** fields for things that may be missing, so the model doesn't invent values.
2. **Enums** for categories.
3. **Validate** in code (Pydantic/Zod), including the rules the API ignores.
4. On a validation failure, **retry once with the error message** included, then route to a person.
5. Measure field-level accuracy on a labelled sample before going live.

sections.heading: Structured output or function calling?
sections.body:
They solve different problems:

- **Structured output** (`response_format`) shapes the model's **final answer** for your code to consume: an extraction, a classification, a report.
- **Function calling** asks **your app to take an action** or fetch data, then continues with the result.

If nothing needs to run and you just want typed data back, use a response schema rather than a fake "submit_answer" tool. Combining structured output with built-in tools (Search, URL context, code execution, File Search, function calling) is a **Preview** feature on Gemini 3 and later models.

keyPoints: `response_format` with `mime_type: application/json` and a `schema` gives schema-shaped JSON.
Length/uniqueness keywords are ignored: validate them yourself.
Nullable fields + descriptions stop the model inventing missing values.
Validate, retry with the error, then escalate.
Schema-valid is not semantically correct: check values (totals, dates) in code.
Structured output shapes the answer; function calling triggers an action.

gotchas.trap: Relying on `maxLength` in the schema to cap a summary field.
gotchas.correct: `maxLength` is stripped silently. Enforce length in your validation code.

gotchas.trap: Making every field required in an extraction schema.
gotchas.correct: Make fields that may be absent nullable, so the model can return null instead of guessing.

gotchas.trap: Assuming schema-constrained JSON means the extracted values are right.
gotchas.correct: The schema guarantees shape, not truth. Add business checks (sums, ranges, cross-field rules) and retry or escalate on failure.

lessons.lab: Write a Pydantic or Zod schema for a receipt (merchant, date, line items, total, currency enum). Extract 10 receipts, validate each, and write a check that the line items add up to the total. Count how often validation catches a problem the schema alone didn't.

lessons.title: Tool design, limits and failure modes
lessons.summary: Keep toolsets lean, stay under schema-complexity limits, mix built-in and custom tools, and recognise the tool-related errors.

sections.heading: A lean, well-named toolset
sections.body:
Tool selection gets worse as the menu grows. The function-calling docs recommend keeping the **active set to about 10 to 20 tools**. If you have more:

- Group tools by task and send only the group the current step needs.
- Merge near-duplicates (`get_order`, `fetch_order`, `lookup_order`) into one tool.
- Use `allowed_tools` to narrow choice for a turn without changing the declarations.

Names should be descriptive and contain no spaces or special characters: use underscores or camelCase. For remote MCP servers, use snake_case server names, because hyphens are not allowed there.

sections.heading: Schema-complexity limits
sections.body:
In `any` mode, or when the parameter schemas are complex, the declarations are compiled into a state machine that constrains decoding. If that grows too big, the request fails with **`400 INVALID_ARGUMENT`**. Retrying will not help. Fix the request:

- Split one big tool into smaller ones.
- Flatten deep nesting.
- Trim long enums and `anyOf` branches.
- Move rules that don't need to be enforced into the **description** instead of the schema.

The same idea applies to response schemas in structured output.

sections.heading: Mixing built-in and custom tools
sections.body:
Gemini 3 and later can combine built-in tools such as Google Search or code execution with your own functions in one request. Server tools run on Google's side and show up as their own steps (for example `google_search_call` / `google_search_result`). Only your `function_call` steps need your code.

Remote MCP servers are declared as `{"type": "mcp_server", "name": ..., "url": ...}`. They must use **Streamable HTTP**; SSE-only servers are not supported. The docs disagree on whether every model supports remote MCP yet, so check the current page before you depend on it.

sections.heading: Errors you will see
sections.body:
Tool-related generation errors include `malformed_function_call`, `malformed_tool_call`, `unexpected_tool_call`, `too_many_tool_calls` and `missing_thought_signature`.

- **Malformed calls**: tighten the schema and descriptions, or use `validated` mode. A known cause is asking the model to write structured text (for example an `<UPDATE>` XML block) right before a tool call. The documented fix is to move those notes into a dedicated function, such as `update(...)`, so they become a call too.
- **Missing thought signature**: in stateless mode you must resend `thought` and `function_call` steps exactly as you received them. Stateful mode (`previous_interaction_id`) and the SDKs handle this for you.
- **Too many tool calls**: check for loops where the model keeps retrying a failing tool. Return a clear error result and keep your own iteration cap.

keyPoints: Keep the active toolset to roughly 10 to 20 tools; narrow per turn with `allowed_tools`.
Names: no spaces or special characters; snake_case for MCP server names (no hyphens).
Over-complex tool schemas give 400 INVALID_ARGUMENT: split, flatten, trim enums/anyOf, move rules to descriptions.
Gemini 3+ can mix built-in tools and custom functions; MCP servers must use Streamable HTTP.
In stateless mode, resend `thought` and `function_call` steps exactly, or you risk `missing_thought_signature`.

gotchas.trap: Retrying with backoff when a large tool schema returns 400 INVALID_ARGUMENT.
gotchas.correct: A 400 means the request is wrong. Simplify the schema (split tools, flatten, trim enums) and resend.

gotchas.trap: Declaring every one of 60 internal APIs on every turn "so the model has options".
gotchas.correct: Send only the tools the current step needs, about 10 to 20 at most, and merge overlapping ones.

gotchas.trap: Prompting the model to emit an XML status block before each tool call.
gotchas.correct: That pattern can cause malformed function calls. Capture the notes in a dedicated `update()` function call instead.

lessons.lab: Take a 30-tool agent and log which tools it picks on 20 test prompts. Group the tools into three task sets of under 10 each, send only the relevant set per step (or use `allowed_tools`), and compare selection accuracy and malformed-call errors before and after.

lessons.title: Grounding with Google Search, Maps and URL context
lessons.summary: Give Gemini fresh, cited facts with built-in grounding tools, render results correctly and control cost.

sections.heading: Turning on Search grounding
sections.body:
Add the built-in tool and the model decides when to search, writes the queries, reads the results and answers with citations:

```python
interaction = client.interactions.create(
    model="gemini-3.8-flash",
    input="Who won the most recent Ballon d'Or?",
    tools=[{"type": "google_search"}],
)
```

The steps include a `google_search_call` (the queries), a `google_search_result` and the `model_output`. Text blocks carry `annotations` of type `url_citation` with `url`, `title` and `start_index`/`end_index`, which tell you exactly which span each source supports.

sections.heading: Display rules and billing
sections.body:
Search grounding comes with terms of service you must follow when you show results:

- **Render the search suggestions.** The `google_search_result` step carries `search_suggestions` HTML (on the legacy API it is `searchEntryPoint`). Show grounded results *with* their suggestions, and only to the end user who sent the prompt.
- **Don't modify the results or mix other content into them.** Don't cache, frame, syndicate, resell, analyze or train on them, and don't add click or link tracking.
- **Limited storage is allowed.** You may keep displayed result text for limited purposes such as the user's chat history (the terms set a maximum period). Read the current terms before you ship.

**Billing.** On Gemini 3 and newer models you pay **per search query the model executes**, not per prompt. One prompt can trigger several queries, and empty queries aren't counted. At the time of writing there is a monthly free allowance shared across Gemini 3+ models, then a per-1,000-query price. Gemini 2.5 and older models were billed per grounded prompt instead. Grounding also has its own rate limits, such as a default daily cap per project.

sections.heading: Other grounding tools
sections.body:
**URL context** (`{"type": "url_context"}`) grounds the answer on pages you name in the prompt, alone or together with Search.

- Each request has a cap on the number of URLs (20 at the time of writing) and a maximum size per URL.
- URLs must be **publicly reachable**: no localhost, private networks or tunnels. Paywalled pages, YouTube, Google Workspace docs and audio/video aren't supported.
- Fetched content is billed as input tokens. Each fetch attempt returns a `url_context_result` step with a status, so check it instead of assuming every page loaded.

**Grounding with Google Maps** (`{"type": "google_maps"}`, with optional `latitude`/`longitude`) answers questions about places, routes and local facts. It is off by default and supports English prompts and responses only. You can combine it with Search on 3.5 Flash and later models.

Maps has its own display rules: the sources **must immediately follow the generated content** and be viewable within one user interaction. Link previews must attribute Google Maps, and the "Google Maps" text must not be altered, wrapped or translated (mark it `translate="no"`). On Gemini 3+ it is billed per query after a shared monthly free allowance, like Search.

Search can be combined with **code execution**, URL context and Maps grounding, and on Gemini 3+ models also with your own **function calling**.

Use Search grounding for **public, current** facts. For your **private** documents, build retrieval (next lesson).

keyPoints: Add `{"type": "google_search"}` to tools; the model decides when to search.
Citations come as `url_citation` annotations with text spans.
Render `search_suggestions` with grounded results, show them only to the requesting user, and don't alter, track or resell them.
Gemini 3+ bills per executed search query (not per prompt), beyond a shared monthly free allowance.
URL context only reads public URLs, with a per-request URL cap; check each `url_context_result` status.
Maps sources must appear immediately after the answer, with unaltered "Google Maps" attribution.

gotchas.trap: Using Google Search grounding to answer questions about your internal HR policies.
gotchas.correct: Search only sees the public web. Use retrieval over your own documents (embeddings + vector search) or put them in context.

gotchas.trap: Showing grounded answers without the search suggestions widget.
gotchas.correct: Render the `search_suggestions` HTML as the grounding terms require.

gotchas.trap: Passing intranet or localhost URLs to URL context.
gotchas.correct: URL context only fetches public URLs. For private pages, retrieve them yourself and put the text in context, or index them for RAG.

gotchas.trap: Putting Maps sources on a separate "Sources" page or translating the "Google Maps" label.
gotchas.correct: Show sources immediately after the generated content, viewable within one interaction, and keep the "Google Maps" text unaltered with `translate="no"`.

gotchas.trap: Estimating Gemini 3+ grounding cost as one charge per prompt.
gotchas.correct: Each executed search query is billed, and one prompt can trigger several. Log the queries in `google_search_call` steps to forecast cost.

lessons.lab: Build a "today in tech" answerer with Search grounding. Print each answer with numbered citations built from the `url_citation` spans, render the search suggestions HTML in a simple web page, and log how many search queries each question triggered.

lessons.title: RAG with Gemini embeddings, and long context
lessons.summary: When to retrieve and when to just use the 1M-token window, and how to build retrieval that cites its sources.

sections.heading: Long context vs retrieval
sections.body:
Gemini 4 Argon has a 1,048,576-token window shared by input, thinking and output. Earlier Gemini 3 and 2.5 models have separate budgets of about 1M tokens in and 64K out. That changes the RAG decision:

- **Small, stable corpus** (a few hundred pages): put it in context, ideally as a stable prefix so implicit caching can kick in. Google calls caching "the primary optimization" for long context. It is simple, and the model sees the whole text instead of only the chunks a retriever picked.
- **Large or fast-changing corpus**, per-user permissions, or strict cost and latency limits: use **retrieval**. Sending hundreds of thousands of tokens on every request is slow and expensive.

Know the accuracy profile too. Finding a **single** fact in a long context is very reliable (about 99% in Google's tests), but accuracy drops when the model must find and combine **many** facts spread across the context. If each answer depends on many scattered details, consider retrieving the relevant parts first, or splitting the work into several focused calls.

sections.heading: Building retrieval
sections.body:
1. **Chunk** documents along their structure (headings, sections), with some overlap.
2. **Embed** chunks with `client.models.embed_content`. `gemini-embedding-2` handles text, images, video, audio and PDF; `gemini-embedding-001` is text-only.
3. **Store** vectors with metadata (source, page, permissions, date).
4. **Retrieve** the top matches, ideally combining vector search with keyword search, then rerank.
5. **Generate**: put the retrieved chunks in the prompt with their ids, and ask the model to answer only from them and cite the ids.
6. **Evaluate** retrieval (was the right chunk retrieved?) separately from generation (was the answer faithful?).

For large re-indexing jobs, the Batch API can create embeddings at a discount.

sections.heading: Embedding options that matter
sections.body:
- **Task hints.** `gemini-embedding-001` takes a `task_type` such as `RETRIEVAL_DOCUMENT`, `RETRIEVAL_QUERY` or `SEMANTIC_SIMILARITY`. `gemini-embedding-2` has **no `task_type`**; instead you put the task in a text prefix (for example `task: search result | query: ...`).
- **Dimensions.** Both models default to 3072 dimensions and support Matryoshka truncation with `output_dimensionality` (768 and 1536 are recommended smaller sizes). Smaller vectors cut storage and search cost. `gemini-embedding-2` normalizes truncated vectors for you; with `gemini-embedding-001` you must normalize them yourself when you use fewer than 3072 dimensions.
- **Spaces are incompatible.** Vectors from `gemini-embedding-001` and `gemini-embedding-2` can't be compared. Upgrading the model means **re-embedding the whole corpus**, not just new documents. Embed queries and documents with the same model and settings.

sections.heading: Managed RAG with File Search
sections.body:
If you don't want to run chunking, a vector store and retrieval yourself, the **File Search** tool does it for you:

```python
tools=[{"type": "file_search", "file_search_store_names": [store.name]}]
```

You upload files into a File Search store, and the model retrieves from it when it needs to. Citations come back as `file_citation` annotations. On pricing, you pay for embeddings at indexing time; storage and query-time embeddings are free. Choose your own pipeline when you need custom chunking, hybrid search, reranking or tight control over permissions.

sections.heading: Prompting over long context
sections.body:
- **Put the documents first and the question last.** Google's guidance is to supply all the context first and place your instructions or question at the very end, anchored with a phrase like "Based on the information above…".
- Label each document with an id and ask for citations by id.
- Ask the model to quote the relevant passage before answering. It improves accuracy and makes answers checkable.
- Tell the model what to do when the answer isn't in the documents ("say you don't know").
- Keep the document block identical across requests and put it at the start, so implicit caching can reuse it.

keyPoints: Small stable corpus → long context (+ implicit caching); large/changing/permissioned corpus → retrieval.
Single-fact recall in long context is very reliable; recalling many scattered facts is less so.
`gemini-embedding-2` is multimodal and has no `task_type` (use a text prefix); `gemini-embedding-001` is text-only and supports `task_type`.
Use `output_dimensionality` to shrink vectors; the two models' embedding spaces are incompatible, so upgrading means re-embedding.
File Search is managed RAG with `file_citation` annotations.
Documents first, question last; allow "I don’t know" and require citations.
Evaluate retrieval and generation separately.

gotchas.trap: Building a vector database for a 40-page handbook that rarely changes.
gotchas.correct: Put the handbook in context as a stable prefix; retrieval adds complexity without benefit here.

gotchas.trap: Blaming the model when answers are wrong, without checking what was retrieved.
gotchas.correct: Log retrieved chunks and measure retrieval recall first; most RAG failures are retrieval failures.

gotchas.trap: Switching new documents to `gemini-embedding-2` while old vectors stay on `gemini-embedding-001`.
gotchas.correct: The spaces are incompatible. Re-embed the whole corpus (and queries) with the new model before switching.

gotchas.trap: Passing `task_type="RETRIEVAL_QUERY"` to `gemini-embedding-2`.
gotchas.correct: It has no `task_type`. Put the task in a text prefix, or use `gemini-embedding-001` if you depend on `task_type`.

gotchas.trap: Putting the question at the top of a 300-page prompt.
gotchas.correct: Put the documents first and the question at the very end.

lessons.lab: Embed 50–100 chunks of a document set with a Gemini embedding model at 768 dimensions and store them in memory. Answer 10 questions with top-5 retrieval and citations. For each wrong answer, record whether the right chunk was retrieved. Then repeat with the whole corpus in context (documents first, question last), and finally with a File Search store, and compare accuracy, latency and cost.

lessons.title: Building agents with the Agent Development Kit (ADK)
lessons.summary: Google's open-source agent framework: agents, tools, workflows, multi-agent teams, sessions, state and memory, callbacks and evaluation.

sections.heading: What ADK is
sections.body:
The **Agent Development Kit** is Google's open-source framework for building, debugging and deploying agents. It's available for Python, TypeScript, Go, Java and Kotlin (`pip install google-adk`, `npm install @google/adk`, and so on). It's model-agnostic but optimised for Gemini. Its docs now live at **adk.dev**.

```python
from google.adk.agents import Agent
from google.adk.tools import google_search

agent = Agent(
    name="researcher",
    model="gemini-3.8-flash",  # pin a stable id in production
    instruction="You help users research topics thoroughly and cite sources.",
    description="Researches topics on the web.",
    tools=[google_search],
)
```

During development you run agents with `adk run` on the command line, `adk web` in a browser UI, or the API server.

sections.heading: The building blocks
sections.body:
- **`Agent` / `LlmAgent`**: `name`, `model`, `instruction`, `description`, `tools`, `sub_agents`, `output_key`.
- **Tools**: function tools (the schema comes from the signature, type hints and docstring, and a parameter with no default is required), **agents-as-tools** (`AgentTool`), long-running function tools, built-ins (Google Search, Code Execution, RAG), and MCP and third-party tools. Add a `ToolContext` parameter when a tool needs to read or write state.
- **Deterministic workflows**: the template agents `SequentialAgent`, `ParallelAgent` and `LoopAgent` orchestrate their children *without consulting a model*. **ADK 2.0** adds **graph-based and dynamic workflows**, and in Python and Go 2.0 these supersede the template workflow agents. Either way, a known step order belongs in a deterministic workflow, not in LLM routing.
- **Callbacks**: `before_/after_agent_callback`, `before_/after_model_callback` and `before_/after_tool_callback`, for logging, guardrails and policy checks.
- **Evaluation**: test agents against an eval set of tasks with expected outcomes before you ship and on every change.

sections.heading: Sessions, state and memory
sections.body:
- A **Session** is one conversation thread: a list of **Events** plus **State** (`session.state`).
- **Memory** is a searchable store that spans sessions. The agent queries it with the `load_memory` tool.
- Pluggable services: `SessionService` (`InMemorySessionService`, `DatabaseSessionService`, `VertexAiSessionService`) and `MemoryService` (`InMemoryMemoryService`, `VertexAiMemoryBankService`, `VertexAiRagMemoryService`). In-memory services lose everything when the process restarts, so use them only in development.

State keys are scoped by prefix:

| Prefix | Scope |
|---|---|
| *(none)* | this session |
| `user:` | all sessions of the same user |
| `app:` | the whole app, every user |
| `temp:` | the current invocation only |

Set `output_key` on an agent to save its final text into state. Write `{key}` in a later agent's instruction to inject that value. This is the standard way to pass results between steps of a workflow.

sections.heading: Multi-agent: sub-agents, AgentTool and A2A
sections.body:
- **Sub-agents**: a coordinator with `sub_agents` gets delegation tools named after each sub-agent, injected automatically. A sub-agent runs in `chat`, `task` or `single_turn` mode, and a task agent calls `finish_task` to hand control back. Write a clear `description` on every sub-agent so the coordinator can tell them apart when it delegates.
- **`AgentTool`**: wraps an agent so another agent calls it like a function and gets the result back, while keeping control of the conversation.
- **A2A (Agent2Agent)**: use it for **remote, independent** agents, such as another team's service, another language, or a third party, that need a formal contract over the network. Prefer local sub-agents when the agents need **shared state or memory**.
- **`ManagedAgent`**: wraps a Google-managed agent (for example Antigravity) through the Interactions API. Its toolset is predefined on the server, so client-side and MCP tools from your ADK app are not supported.

sections.heading: Design advice
sections.body:
- Start with **one agent and a few good tools**. Add a deterministic workflow when the steps are known in advance, and add multi-agent only when the work is truly separable.
- Put **hard rules in code** (callbacks, tool checks), not only in the instruction.
- Define **stop conditions** and an iteration or budget cap, especially for loops.
- Use the right state scope: `user:` for preferences, `temp:` for scratch values, and Memory for recall across sessions.
- Build an **eval set** of tasks with expected outcomes, and run it on every change.

keyPoints: ADK: open source, Python/TypeScript/Go/Java/Kotlin, model-agnostic, Gemini-optimised; docs at adk.dev.
Template workflow agents (Sequential, Parallel, Loop) run without consulting a model; ADK 2.0 graph workflows supersede them in Python/Go 2.0.
State prefixes: none = session, `user:`, `app:`, `temp:`. `output_key` writes the final text into state, and `{key}` reads it back.
Sub-agents for local, shared-state teams; `AgentTool` to call an agent like a function; A2A for remote or third-party agents.
Callbacks (agent, model, tool) for deterministic guardrails; evals before deploying.

gotchas.trap: Starting with a five-agent hierarchy for a task with three fixed steps.
gotchas.correct: Use a deterministic workflow (a SequentialAgent, or a graph workflow in ADK 2.0) or a single agent. Add agents only when evals show the need.

gotchas.trap: Enforcing "never refund over $500" only in the agent instruction.
gotchas.correct: Enforce it in the tool or in a `before_tool_callback` so it holds every time.

gotchas.trap: Storing a user's language preference under a plain state key and expecting it in their next session.
gotchas.correct: Plain keys are session-scoped. Use the `user:` prefix and a persistent SessionService.

gotchas.trap: Wiring a vendor's remotely hosted agent in as a local sub-agent.
gotchas.correct: Remote, independently owned agents with a formal contract are an A2A use case.

lessons.lab: Build an ADK agent with two function tools (search a local FAQ, create a ticket) and a `before_tool_callback` that blocks ticket creation without an email address. Store the user's preferred language under `user:language`, and use `output_key` plus `{key}` templating to pass a classification into the answering step of a deterministic workflow. Write five eval cases and run them.

lessons.title: Managed Agents and the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform
lessons.summary: Call Google-hosted agents such as Antigravity and Deep Research through the Interactions API, and deploy your own agents on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.

sections.heading: Google-managed agents via the Interactions API
sections.body:
**Managed Agents** are in **Public Preview** (launched May 2026). One call provisions a Google-hosted, OS-isolated Linux sandbox in which the agent works. You call them through the same Interactions API by passing `agent` instead of only a model.

- **Antigravity** runs code and works with files inside the sandbox, and can search and read web pages. Its default tools are code execution, Google Search and URL context. You can add your own function tools and an MCP server.
- **Deep Research** plans and runs multi-step research across many sources and returns a cited report. There is a faster id and a more thorough "max" id.

```python
interaction = client.interactions.create(
    agent="antigravity-preview-09-2026",
    input="Audit our public docs site for broken links and summarise the fixes as a table.",
    environment="remote",            # or an environment id to reuse files and state
    agent_config={"type": "antigravity", "model": "gemini-4-argon"},
    background=True,                  # long-running: poll for the result
    store=True,                       # background mode requires stored interactions
)
```

Agent ids are preview ids that get replaced. An older Antigravity id has already been shut down, so check the current id before you ship.

sections.heading: Running managed agents safely and reliably
sections.body:
- **Background execution**: Antigravity runs with `background=True`, and Deep Research *requires* it. Background mode needs `store=True`. Poll `interactions.get` until the status is final, or stream with `stream=True` and reconnect with `last_event_id` after a drop. A Deep Research task can run up to an hour, though most finish much sooner.
- **Network**: outbound access from the sandbox is **unrestricted by default**. Restrict it with a `network` allowlist.
- **Secrets**: store them as **managed credentials**, which an egress proxy injects. Never paste them into the prompt or files.
- **Deep Research limits**: no custom function tools and **no structured output**. If you need JSON, run a normal model call with `response_format` on the finished report. You can add an MCP server or file search.
- **Customising Antigravity**: mount `.agents/AGENTS.md`, which is loaded as system instructions in addition to any `system_instruction`, and skills under `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`. Save a configuration as a reusable agent with `client.agents.create(...)`. The model is locked when you create it.
- **Limits**: Antigravity compacts context when it grows large. A `max_total_tokens` cap ends the run with `status: "incomplete"`, and inputs are text and inline images only.
- **Cost**: billed pay-as-you-go on model tokens and tool use. Deep Research tasks cost far more than a single grounded call, so use it when depth matters.

On **April 22 2026** Vertex AI became part of the **Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform** ("Vertex AI is now part of Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform"). You'll still see the old names in blog posts and code:

Use the Agent Platform when the workload needs to run inside a governed Google Cloud project: IAM, audit logging, network and encryption controls, and managed sessions and memory. sections.heading: Deploying ADK agents
sections.body:
ADK agents can run on any container host. On Google Cloud the documented targets are:

- **GKE**: when you already run a Kubernetes platform.

The separate **Agents CLI** (`agents-cli deploy`) sets up CI/CD and infrastructure as code. For production, back sessions and memory with persistent services (for example Agent Platform Sessions and Memory Bank) instead of in-memory ones.
