questions.stem: After you send a prompt with function declarations, Gemini returns a `function_call` step. What happens next?
options: Your application validates the arguments, runs the function and sends a `function_result` with the matching `call_id`
Gemini runs the function on Google’s servers and returns the result
Gemini waits for a webhook from your server
The interaction is complete; you show the call to the user
questions.explanation: The model only proposes calls. Your code executes them and returns `function_result` steps linked by `call_id`.
rationales: Correct.
Gemini never executes your functions.
You send the result back in the next request.
You must return the result so the model can answer.

questions.stem: You need the model to always call one of your tools on this turn, never answer in plain text. Which `tool_choice` fits?
options: `required_text`
`none`
`auto`
`any`
questions.explanation: `tool_choice: "any"` forces a function call; `auto` lets the model choose; `none` blocks calls; `validated` enforces schema adherence. If you also need to limit which functions are eligible, use the `allowed_tools` object form.
rationales: Not a mode.
Prohibits calls.
Lets the model decide, so it may answer directly.
Correct: the model must predict a function call.

questions.stem: The model returns three `function_call` steps in one turn (weather for three cities). What should your code do?
options: Merge them into one call with three cities
Reject parallel calls by setting `tool_choice: none`
Run all three and return all three `function_result` steps, each with its own `call_id`
Run only the first; the model will ask again for the others
questions.explanation: Parallel calls are independent. Execute each and return every result, matched by `call_id`.
rationales: Changes the contract the model asked for.
Disables tools entirely.
Correct.
It expects all results.

questions.scenario: Support assistant with live order data
questions.stem: A `cancel_order` tool must never run for orders already shipped. Where should that rule be enforced?
options: Only in the system instruction
In the function description
By setting `tool_choice: none`
In the tool’s own code, which checks shipping status before cancelling
questions.explanation: Business rules that must always hold belong in code. Descriptions and instructions help the model choose but cannot guarantee behaviour.
rationales: Prompts make it likely, not guaranteed.
Descriptions guide choice; they do not enforce.
That disables all tools.
Correct: deterministic enforcement.

questions.stem: Which two make a function declaration more likely to be chosen correctly? (Select two.)
options: A description that says what the tool does and when to use it
Parameters with enums and clear descriptions
A very short, generic name like `do`
Many overlapping tools for the same job
questions.explanation: Clear descriptions and precise schemas are the main levers for correct tool selection. Keep toolsets small and distinct.
rationales: Correct.
Correct.
Vague names hurt selection.
Overlap confuses selection.

questions.stem: How do you ask Gemini for JSON that matches a schema in the Interactions API?
options: Use the Files API to upload a schema
Set `response_format` with `mime_type: "application/json"` and a `schema`
Add "respond in JSON" to the prompt and parse whatever comes back
Set `tool_choice: none`
questions.explanation: Structured output uses `response_format` with a JSON MIME type and a schema (for example from Pydantic or Zod). Prompt-only requests for JSON are not schema-guaranteed.
rationales: Schemas go in `response_format`.
Correct.
Works sometimes; not schema-guaranteed.
Unrelated.

questions.stem: Your schema sets `maxLength: 200` on a summary field, but you sometimes get 400-character summaries. Why?
options: The schema was too complex and was ignored entirely
Thinking was set too high
`maxLength` is one of the keywords Gemini strips silently, so you must enforce it in code
`maxLength` counts tokens, not characters
questions.explanation: Gemini ignores length and uniqueness keywords such as `minLength`, `maxLength` and `uniqueItems`. Validate them in your application.
rationales: Complex schemas are rejected with 400, not ignored.
Unrelated.
Correct.
It is ignored, not reinterpreted.

questions.stem: Invoices sometimes lack a due date, and the model invents one. What schema change helps most?
options: Make `due_date` required
Remove the field and parse dates with regex later
Add `minLength: 10` to the field
Make `due_date` nullable (for example `["string", "null"]`) and describe when to return null
questions.explanation: Nullable fields let the model say "not present" instead of guessing. Pair them with a description that says when to use null.
rationales: Forces a value, encouraging invention.
Loses a field the model can extract when present.
Ignored, and it would push toward invented values anyway.
Correct.

questions.stem: A deeply nested schema with many unions fails with `400 INVALID_ARGUMENT`. What should you do?
options: Simplify the schema: flatten the nesting, reduce unions and trim long enums
Retry the same request with backoff
Switch to the Batch API
Raise thinking_level to high
questions.explanation: Overly complex schemas are rejected with 400 INVALID_ARGUMENT. Simplify the schema (flatten nesting, reduce unions, trim enums); retrying the same request will not help.
rationales: Correct, per the docs.
400 means fix the request.
Batch does not relax schema-complexity limits; a 400 needs a simpler schema.
Thinking level does not change schema-complexity limits.

questions.stem: Which pattern is the most reliable way to turn documents into validated records?
options: Ask the model to grade its own output and skip validation
Schema with descriptions and nullable fields, validate in code, retry once with the validation error, then route to a person
Trust schema-constrained output without validation
Retry failed records indefinitely until they validate
questions.explanation: Constrained output plus code validation plus a bounded retry and human fallback is the dependable extraction loop. Schema-valid output can still contain wrong values, and some schema keywords are ignored, so code validation is required.
rationales: Self-grading is not validation.
Correct.
Some constraints are ignored, and values can still be wrong.
Unbounded retries waste money and may never pass.

questions.stem: Which statements about Gemini structured output are correct? (Select three.)
options: Recursive schemas can use `$ref`
`uniqueItems` is enforced on arrays
`anyOf` is supported for alternative object shapes
String `enum` values can restrict a field to fixed categories
questions.explanation: Gemini supports enums, `anyOf` and recursive `$ref`, among others. Uniqueness and length keywords are ignored.
rationales: Correct.
It is silently ignored.
Correct.
Correct.

questions.stem: In a compositional flow (get forecast → set thermostat), what should your loop include besides executing calls?
options: A rule to stop after the first call
Parsing the model’s text for the word "done"
`tool_choice: any` on every turn
A maximum number of iterations as a safety net
questions.explanation: Keep looping while the model asks for calls, and add an iteration cap so a misbehaving loop cannot run forever. The loop ends when a turn comes back with no further `function_call` steps.
rationales: Compositional flows need several calls.
Use the absence of further calls, not text parsing.
Would force calls even when the model should answer.
Correct.

questions.stem: A tool call fails because the customer id does not exist. What should the `function_result` contain?
options: A clear error message saying what failed and what to try next
An empty string
Nothing; skip sending a result
A made-up placeholder customer
questions.explanation: Return actionable errors in the result so the model can ask the user or try another approach. An empty or missing result leaves the model guessing, and a placeholder invents data.
rationales: Correct: the model can recover.
The model may misread it as success or no data.
The model is waiting for it.
Invents data.

questions.stem: You poll a background interaction and see `status: "requires_action"`. What does your worker need to do?
options: Wait longer; the model is still generating
Run the requested function(s) and send back `function_result` steps with the matching `call_id`s
Cancel the interaction, because it has failed
Raise `thinking_level` and resubmit the same input
questions.explanation: A `function_call` puts the interaction into `requires_action`: the model is waiting for your code to execute the call. Your worker runs it and replies with `function_result` steps linked by `call_id`. Polling longer will never change the status on its own.
rationales: That would be `in_progress`; this status waits on you.
Correct: the model is blocked on your tool results.
Failures show as `failed`, not `requires_action`.
Nothing is wrong with the reasoning; it needs a result.

questions.stem: Your streaming handler calls `transfer_funds` with whatever it can parse from the first `arguments_delta` event, and occasionally sends an amount of `1` instead of `1500`. What is the fix?
options: Turn off streaming whenever tools are declared
Set `tool_choice: "validated"` so deltas arrive complete
Aggregate the `arguments_delta` partial JSON until the call step stops, then parse, validate and (for money movement) confirm before executing
Ask the model in the system instruction to send arguments in a single delta
questions.explanation: Streamed tool arguments arrive as partial JSON fragments that must be joined before you act on them. Executing on the first fragment reads a truncated value. Validation and confirmation are still needed for a high-impact action like a transfer.
rationales: Works, but throws away streaming instead of handling it correctly.
`validated` concerns schema adherence, not how deltas are chunked.
Correct.
Prompts cannot control stream chunking.

questions.scenario: Triage step in a support workflow
questions.stem: At the triage step you must make the model call either `route_to_billing` or `route_to_tech`, never answer in text and never call any of your other eight tools. What is the cleanest Interactions API setting?
options: `tool_choice: "auto"` plus a system instruction listing the two allowed tools
`tool_choice: {"allowed_tools": {"mode": "any", "tools": ["route_to_billing", "route_to_tech"]}}`
`tool_choice: "none"` and parse the routing decision from the text
`tool_choice: "any"` with all ten tools declared
questions.explanation: The object form of `tool_choice` combines "must call" with a restricted list of functions. Plain `any` forces a call but allows any declared tool. Instructions alone do not guarantee the restriction.
rationales: `auto` lets the model answer in text or pick another tool.
Correct: forced call, limited to the two routing tools.
Prohibits calls and relies on parsing free text.
Forces a call, but any of the ten tools could be chosen.

questions.stem: A legacy generateContent app declares functions and also enables Google Search, without setting `function_calling_config`. Which mode applies by default, and what does it do?
options: `AUTO`; the model decides with no schema enforcement
`ANY`; the model must call a function every turn
`NONE`; custom functions are disabled while built-in tools are on
`VALIDATED`; the model predicts calls or text and enforces the function schema
questions.explanation: `VALIDATED` is the default mode for tool combination, when built-in tools or structured output are enabled alongside functions. It reduces malformed calls compared with `AUTO`. `AUTO` is the default only when function declarations are the only tools.
rationales: `AUTO` is the default when only function declarations are present.
`ANY` is never the default.
`NONE` is equivalent to sending no declarations; it is not a default.
Correct.

questions.stem: Your assistant declares 45 tools on every turn, and it often picks the wrong one of several similar lookups. Which change addresses the root cause?
options: Raise `thinking_level` to high on every request
Merge overlapping tools and send only the 10 to 20 relevant to the current task
Shorten each tool description to one word to save tokens
Switch `tool_choice` to `any`
questions.explanation: The docs recommend an active set of about 10 to 20 tools with clear, non-overlapping purposes. A large menu of similar tools confuses selection. More thinking or forced calls do not remove the ambiguity.
rationales: Costs more without fixing the overlapping menu.
Correct.
Descriptions are the main signal for choosing; shrinking them hurts.
Forces a call but does not help pick the right one.

questions.stem: A request in `any` mode with one large tool (deep nesting, a 300-value enum and many `anyOf` branches) fails with `400 INVALID_ARGUMENT`. Which two changes are appropriate? (Select two.)
options: Split the tool into smaller tools and flatten the nesting
Retry with exponential backoff until it succeeds
Trim the enum and `anyOf` branches, moving non-critical rules into the description
Move the request to the Batch API, which allows larger schemas
questions.explanation: In `any` mode or with complex schemas, declarations compile to a state machine, and exceeding its limits returns 400. The documented fixes are to split tools, flatten nesting, trim enums and `anyOf`, and move rules into descriptions. A 400 is a request problem, so retries will not help.
rationales: Correct.
400 errors are not transient.
Correct.
Batch does not relax schema-complexity limits; the schema itself must be simplified.

questions.stem: Every response passes your Pydantic schema, yet audits find invoices where `total` doesn't equal the sum of `line_items`. What is the best next step?
options: Add `uniqueItems` and `maxLength` to the schema
Nothing; schema-valid output is guaranteed to be correct
Make every field required
Add a business-rule check (line items sum to total); on failure retry once with the error, then route to a person
questions.explanation: Structured output guarantees valid JSON in the schema's shape, not semantically correct values. Cross-field rules must be checked in code. A bounded retry with the error message plus human fallback handles the misses.
rationales: Those keywords are ignored and would not check arithmetic anyway.
Shape is guaranteed; correctness is not.
Encourages invented values and does nothing for the sum.
Correct.

questions.stem: You want each ticket returned as `{category, priority, summary}` for your database. Nothing needs to be executed. A teammate proposes declaring a `save_ticket` function and forcing it with `tool_choice: "any"`. What do you recommend?
options: Use `response_format` with a JSON schema, because structured output formats the final answer and no action is needed
Keep the forced function; it is the only way to get typed fields
Ask for JSON in the prompt and parse it with regex
Use `tool_choice: "none"` with the function declared
questions.explanation: Structured output is for shaping the final answer your code consumes; function calling is for asking your app to take an action. A response schema is the direct fit and avoids a fake tool round trip. Prompt-only JSON has no schema guarantee.
rationales: Correct.
Response schemas also give typed fields.
No schema guarantee and fragile parsing.
Blocks calls and gives you no structured output.

questions.stem: How do you let Gemini answer with current, cited web information?
options: Use a Live model
Upload yesterday’s news with the Files API
Set `thinking_level` to high
Add `{"type": "google_search"}` to `tools`
questions.explanation: Grounding with Google Search lets the model search, read results and cite sources.
rationales: Live models are for real-time streaming sessions; they don't add web grounding by themselves.
Static and quickly stale.
Thinking does not add web access.
Correct.

questions.stem: Where are citations for a Search-grounded answer exposed?
options: Only in the AI Studio UI
In the `usage` object
As `url_citation` annotations on text blocks, with url, title and start/end indexes
In a footnote string appended to `output_text` only

rationales: They are in the API response.
`usage` reports tokens.
Correct.
The structured annotations are the reliable source.

A link to AI Studio

Enable Google Search grounding

rationales: URL context only fetches public URLs; intranet addresses and private networks aren't reachable.
Correct: private data needs your own retrieval.
Search only sees the public web.
The model has never seen them.

questions.stem: A 60-page product manual changes twice a year. Users ask questions about it. What is the simplest effective design?
options: Fine-tune a model on the manual
Use Google Search grounding
Put the manual in context as a stable prefix and let implicit caching reduce cost
Build a vector database with hybrid search and reranking
questions.explanation: For a small, stable corpus, long context is simpler and often more accurate than retrieval; implicit caching keeps repeated prefixes cheap.
rationales: Costly and harder to update.
The manual may not be public, and search adds cost.
Correct.
Overkill for a small, stable document.

questions.stem: Which Gemini embedding model can embed images, video, audio and PDF as well as text?
options: `gemini-embedding-001`
`gemini-3.8-flash`
`gemini-3.5-flash-lite`
`gemini-embedding-2`
questions.explanation: `gemini-embedding-2` is multimodal; `gemini-embedding-001` handles text.
rationales: Text only.
A generative model, not an embedding model.
A generative Flash-Lite model, not an embedding model.
Correct.

questions.stem: A RAG assistant gives wrong answers. What should you check first?
options: Whether the right chunks were retrieved for those questions
Whether thinking_level is high enough
Whether the system instruction is long enough
Whether the embeddings use the newest model, and switch immediately
questions.explanation: Log retrieved chunks and measure retrieval recall separately from answer faithfulness.
rationales: Correct: most RAG failures are retrieval failures.
Reasoning cannot fix missing evidence.
Unlikely root cause.
Measure before changing components.

questions.stem: Which two prompt habits make long-context answers easier to audit? (Select two.)
options: Ask for the answer with no explanation to save tokens
Label each document with an id and require citations by id
Ask the model to quote the supporting passage before answering
Put the question before the documents
questions.explanation: Ids with citations by id, and a supporting quote before the answer, make long-context answers checkable. Google's guidance also puts the documents first and the question last.
rationales: Harder to audit.
Correct.
Correct.
Documents first, question last.

questions.stem: You want answers grounded in three specific public web pages your team picked. Which tool fits best?
options: Code execution
The Batch API
URL context
Google Maps grounding
questions.explanation: URL context grounds responses on specific URLs, alone or combined with Search.
rationales: Runs code, does not fetch your chosen pages.
A cost mode, not a grounding tool.
Correct: grounds on URLs you provide.
For places and routes.

questions.scenario: Restaurant finder in a travel app
questions.stem: A travel app uses Grounding with Google Maps to recommend restaurants. The design team wants to keep the answer clean by moving the Maps sources to a "Sources" tab and showing the label as "Google Maps" translated into the user's language. What should you do?
options: Ship the design; Maps attribution rules only apply to embedded map widgets
Show the sources immediately after the generated content, viewable within one interaction, and keep the "Google Maps" text unaltered with `translate="no"`
Drop the sources entirely and add a single footer credit to Google
Switch to Google Search grounding, which has no display requirements
questions.explanation: Maps grounding requires sources to immediately follow the generated content and be viewable within one user interaction. The "Google Maps" attribution text must not be altered, wrapped or localized, so mark it `translate="no"`.
rationales: The rules apply to Maps-grounded answers, not only to map widgets.
Correct: this meets both the placement and the attribution rules.
A generic footer doesn't satisfy the source display rule.
Search grounding has its own display rules (search suggestions), and it is a worse fit for places and local facts.

sources.title: Grounding with Google Maps — Gemini API docs

questions.stem: An analyst assistant uses the URL context tool. Users report that some pages are "ignored". Which two inputs would URL context fail to use? (Select two.)
options: A public product page served as HTML
A page on the company intranet at `http://wiki.internal/pricing`
A public PDF datasheet
A YouTube product demo video
questions.explanation: URL context only fetches publicly reachable URLs, so private networks, localhost and tunnels fail. YouTube, Workspace docs, paywalled pages and audio/video aren't supported, while HTML and PDF are. Check each `url_context_result` status to see which fetches failed.
rationales: HTML is supported.
Correct: private network addresses aren't reachable.
PDF is a supported type.
Correct: YouTube and audio/video content aren't supported by URL context.

questions.stem: A team has 2 million chunks indexed with `gemini-embedding-001`. To save time, they plan to embed only new documents and incoming queries with `gemini-embedding-2` and keep the old vectors. What will happen, and what should they do?
options: Search quality improves gradually as old documents age out; no action needed
Search breaks, because the two models' embedding spaces are incompatible; re-embed the whole corpus with `gemini-embedding-2` (the Batch API keeps the cost down)
It works if they set `output_dimensionality` to 3072 on both models
It works if they pass `task_type="RETRIEVAL_QUERY"` to `gemini-embedding-2` for queries
questions.explanation: Vectors from `gemini-embedding-001` and `gemini-embedding-2` live in different spaces and can't be compared. Upgrading means re-embedding the whole corpus, and batch embeddings are cheaper for a bulk job like this.
rationales: New queries won't match old vectors in a meaningful way, so most results will be wrong.
Correct.
Matching dimension counts doesn't make the spaces compatible.
`gemini-embedding-2` has no `task_type`, and task hints can't bridge two spaces anyway.

questions.stem: You are moving a retrieval pipeline from `gemini-embedding-001` to `gemini-embedding-2`. The old code passes `task_type="RETRIEVAL_QUERY"` for queries and `RETRIEVAL_DOCUMENT` for chunks. How do you carry this intent over?
options: Keep the same `task_type` values; both models accept them
Drop the task hints; embeddings never benefit from them
Express the task as a text prefix on the input (for example `task: search result | query: ...`), since `gemini-embedding-2` has no `task_type`
Use different `output_dimensionality` values for queries and documents
questions.explanation: `gemini-embedding-2` does not support `task_type`. Google's guidance is to state the task in a text prefix on the input instead.
rationales: Only `gemini-embedding-001` supports `task_type`.
Task hints help retrieval; the new model takes them as a prefix.
Correct.
Queries and documents must use the same dimensions to be compared.

questions.stem: A RAG index on `gemini-embedding-001` uses the default 3072-dimension vectors, and vector database costs are too high. Which change reduces storage while keeping one consistent index?
options: Re-embed everything with `output_dimensionality=768`, normalize the vectors, and embed queries at 768 too
Keep 3072 for documents and use 768 for queries
Switch to a generative model's hidden states
Cut chunks to one sentence each so there are fewer vectors
questions.explanation: Gemini embeddings support Matryoshka truncation through `output_dimensionality`, and 768 is a recommended size. With `gemini-embedding-001`, vectors below 3072 dimensions must be normalized manually, and queries must use the same size as documents.
rationales: Correct.
Vectors of different sizes can't be compared.
Not an available or sensible embedding approach.
One-sentence chunks give more vectors, not fewer, and lose context.

questions.stem: A two-person team needs a Gemini assistant over a few thousand internal PDFs that grow every week. They don't want to run chunking, a vector database or retrieval code, and they need citations. Which option fits best?
options: Google Search grounding with the PDFs published on a hidden web page
The File Search tool with a File Search store; citations come back as `file_citation` annotations
Put all the PDFs in every request
Fine-tune a model on the PDFs each week
questions.explanation: File Search is managed RAG: you upload files to a store, the model retrieves from it, and citations come back as `file_citation` annotations. You pay for embeddings at indexing time, while storage and query-time embeddings are free.
rationales: Publishing private documents to rely on web search is unsafe and unreliable.
Correct.
A growing corpus of thousands of PDFs won't fit, and every request would be slow and costly.
Fine-tuning doesn't give citations and is costly to repeat weekly.

questions.stem: An auditor sends 400 contracts (about 600K tokens) in one request and asks Gemini to list every contract with an auto-renewal clause and its notice period. Spot checks show some contracts are missed, though single-contract questions are answered well. What is the best explanation and fix?
options: The context window is exceeded; the fix is a model with a bigger window
Long-context recall is very reliable for one fact but drops when many facts spread across the context must be found; extract per contract (or retrieve relevant clauses) and then aggregate
Raising `temperature` will make the model explore more contracts
The model ignores documents placed before the question; put the question first
questions.explanation: Google reports about 99% accuracy for finding a single fact in long context, but lower accuracy when many facts must be found. A task that needs a result for every contract is a many-fact task, so split it into per-contract calls or retrieve candidate clauses first, then combine the results.
rationales: 600K tokens fits in a 1M-token window; the issue is recall, not capacity.
Correct.
Sampling parameters are ignored on the newest models and don't fix recall.
The guidance is the reverse: documents first, question last.

questions.stem: A product review of a Search-grounded news assistant lists proposed features. Which two would violate the grounding terms? (Select two.)
options: Rendering the `search_suggestions` HTML next to each grounded answer
Adding click tracking to the result links and suggestions to measure engagement
Saving grounded results to train an internal ranking model
Keeping the displayed answer text in the user's own chat history
questions.explanation: The terms forbid click or link tracking on results and suggestions, and forbid analyzing or training on results. Rendering search suggestions is required, and limited storage of displayed text for purposes such as the user's chat history is allowed.
rationales: This is required, not a violation.
Correct: click and link tracking is not allowed.
Correct: training on grounded results is not allowed.
Storing displayed text for the user's chat history is a permitted, limited use.

questions.stem: A team on Gemini 3.8 Flash forecasts Search grounding cost as "number of grounded prompts × per-query price". Actual spend is much higher. What is the most likely reason?
options: Grounding is billed per output token
Search grounding is billed per prompt only on Gemini 3+ models, so the forecast should be correct
On Gemini 3+ each executed search query is billed, and one prompt can trigger several queries
Thinking tokens are charged at the search price
questions.explanation: On Gemini 3 and newer models, Search grounding is billed per search query the model executes, after a monthly free allowance. One prompt can run several queries, so count queries from the `google_search_call` steps when forecasting.
rationales: Output tokens are billed separately; grounding is billed per query.
Per-prompt billing applied to Gemini 2.5 and older, not 3+.
Correct.
Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens, not as searches.

questions.stem: What is the Agent Development Kit (ADK)?
options: A paid Workspace add-on for end users
A model id for agentic tasks
A Google Cloud console for billing
Google’s open-source framework for building, debugging and deploying agents
questions.explanation: ADK is open source, available in Python, TypeScript, Go, Java and Kotlin, and optimised for Gemini while model-agnostic.

Unrelated.

questions.stem: A process always runs three fixed steps in order: extract, validate, summarise. Each step needs a model call, but the order never changes. How should you orchestrate it in ADK?
options: A deterministic workflow: a SequentialAgent, or a graph workflow in ADK 2.0
A LoopAgent that repeats until the summary looks good
A coordinator LLM agent that decides which sub-agent to call next
A ParallelAgent running all three steps at once
questions.explanation: When the step order is known in advance, orchestrate it deterministically. Template workflow agents run their children without consulting a model, and in ADK 2.0 (Python and Go) graph workflows supersede them for the same job. LLM routing adds cost and nondeterminism with no benefit here.
rationales: Correct: fixed order, deterministic orchestration.
A loop repeats until a condition. These steps run once each.
LLM routing for a fixed order adds cost and lets the model skip or reorder steps.
The steps depend on each other, so they cannot run in parallel.

A higher thinking level
A sentence in the agent instruction
A callback or tool check in code that blocks the action
questions.explanation: Callbacks and tool code give deterministic guardrails; instructions only influence behaviour.
rationales: Guides but does not enforce.
Does not enforce rules.
Not guaranteed.

questions.stem: How do you call a Google-managed agent such as Antigravity through the Interactions API?
options: Use `tool_choice: any`
Call it through the Batch API only
Pass `agent="..."` with its configuration to `client.interactions.create`
Deploy it yourself on GKE first

rationales: Unrelated.
Not required.

questions.stem: A Deep Research task can take several minutes, sometimes far longer. How should the app call it?
options: Use background execution and poll the interaction until it completes
Hold an HTTP request open with a 30-second timeout
Use `store=False`
Split it into dozens of short Flash calls run in sequence
questions.explanation: Deep Research requires `background=True`, which needs stored interactions. Poll `interactions.get` until the status is final, or stream and reconnect with `last_event_id`.
rationales: Correct.
A long synchronous request will time out, and Deep Research requires background mode anyway.
Background mode requires `store=True`.
You lose the managed agent's planning and citations.

questions.stem: An ADK support agent asks each user for their preferred language once. The value should apply in every future conversation with that user, but never leak to other users. Where should the agent store it?
options: Under a plain state key such as `language`
Under `app:language`
Under `user:language`, with a persistent SessionService
Under `temp:language`
questions.explanation: The `user:` prefix scopes state to all sessions of the same user. Plain keys last only for the current session, `app:` is shared by every user, and `temp:` lasts one invocation. The value also needs a persistent SessionService, because in-memory services lose it on restart.
rationales: Session-scoped: lost when the next conversation starts.
App-wide: one user's setting would apply to everyone.
Correct.
Discarded after the current invocation.

questions.stem: In an ADK workflow, a classifier agent runs first and an answering agent second. What is the standard way to get the classifier's result into the answering agent's instruction?
options: Set `output_key="category"` on the classifier and write `{category}` in the answering agent's instruction
Make the answering agent call the classifier again as its first tool call
Concatenate both instructions into one long system prompt
Write the result to a local file and read it in a callback
questions.explanation: `output_key` saves an agent's final text into session state, and `{key}` templating injects state into another agent's instruction. This passes data between workflow steps without extra model calls or side channels.
rationales: Correct.
Repeats work and doubles cost.
Merges two roles and drops the workflow structure.
A fragile side channel. Session state is built for this.

questions.stem: Your Python ADK travel agent needs to book through a hotel partner's booking agent. The partner hosts it, writes it in Java, and publishes a formal interface. Your agent does not need the partner's internal state. How should you integrate it?
options: Copy the partner's code into your repo and add it as a local sub-agent
Connect to it with A2A (Agent2Agent)
Put the partner's API docs in your agent's instruction and let the model write HTTP calls
Wrap your own agent in an `AgentTool` and send it to the partner
questions.explanation: A2A is meant for remote, independently owned, cross-language or third-party agents with a formal contract. Local sub-agents fit when agents share state or memory in one app, which is not the case here.
rationales: You do not own or run the partner's agent, and it is in another language.
Correct.
Unreliable and unsafe: the contract should live in code, not in prose.
Backwards: `AgentTool` wraps a local agent for your own agent to call.

questions.stem: A team uses the Deep Research agent and wants (1) the result as JSON matching a strict schema for their database, and (2) the agent to call their internal `lookup_customer` function during research. What should you tell them?
options: Pass `response_format` and add `lookup_customer` as a function tool in the Deep Research call
Switch to `deep-research-max` to unlock functions and schemas
Neither is supported by Deep Research. Run a separate model call with `response_format` on the finished report, and use an agent that supports custom functions if the research needs them
Set `tool_choice` to `any` so Deep Research calls the function
questions.explanation: Deep Research does not support custom function tools or structured output. Convert its report with a normal structured-output call, or use an agent that accepts custom functions, such as Antigravity.
rationales: Both features are unsupported on Deep Research.
The max variant is more thorough but has the same limits.
Correct.
`tool_choice` cannot add a feature the agent does not support.

questions.stem: An Antigravity agent will call your company's internal ticketing API with an API token. Security requires that the sandbox can reach only that API and that the token never appears in prompts or files. Which two measures meet this? (Select two.)
options: Configure a `network` allowlist for the sandbox that permits only the ticketing API host
Rely on the default sandbox settings, which block outbound traffic
Store the token as a managed credential, which the egress proxy injects
Put the token in `.agents/AGENTS.md` so the agent knows to use it
questions.explanation: Outbound network access from a managed-agent sandbox is unrestricted by default, so you need a `network` allowlist. Managed credentials let the egress proxy inject secrets without exposing them to the model or the filesystem.
rationales: Correct.
Wrong: egress is unrestricted by default.
Correct.
AGENTS.md is loaded as system instructions, so the token would be exposed to the model.

questions.stem: A developer calls Antigravity with `background=True` and `store=False`, and the request fails. What is the fix?
options: Remove `environment="remote"`
Switch the model to Flash-Lite
Lower the thinking level
Set `store=True`, because background execution needs stored interactions
questions.explanation: Background mode keeps the interaction on the server so you can poll or resume it, so it requires `store=True`. The environment, model and thinking level are unrelated to this error.
rationales: The remote environment is how Antigravity runs.
The model choice does not affect the storage requirement.
Unrelated.
Correct.

sources.title: Interactions API overview — Gemini API docs

questions.stem: Several teams should run the same Antigravity setup: house coding rules, two custom skills and a fixed model. What is the best approach?
options: Paste the rules and skill text into every user prompt
Mount `.agents/AGENTS.md` and `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, then save the configuration as a reusable agent with `client.agents.create`
Fine-tune a Flash model on the coding rules
Build an ADK `ManagedAgent` and pass the skills as client-side MCP tools
questions.explanation: Antigravity loads `.agents/AGENTS.md` as system instructions and picks up skills under `.agents/skills/`. `client.agents.create` saves the whole configuration as a reusable agent, with the model locked at creation.
rationales: Repetitive and easy to drift, and it uses tokens on every call.
Correct.
Heavy, and it does not configure the managed agent.
ADK `ManagedAgent` does not support client-side or MCP tools.

questions.stem: An ADK agent can call `issue_refund(amount)`. Policy says refunds over a set limit must never execute without human approval, even if the model is convinced otherwise. Where should you enforce this?
options: In a `before_tool_callback` (or in the tool itself) that blocks the call above the limit
In an `after_model_callback` that rewrites the final answer text
In the agent `instruction`, in capital letters
By raising the thinking level so the model reasons more carefully
questions.explanation: A `before_tool_callback` runs in code before every tool call and can block it deterministically. Instructions and thinking only influence the model. An after-model text rewrite does not stop the tool from running.
rationales: Correct.
Too late and in the wrong place: the refund call is not intercepted.
Influences the model but does not enforce the rule.
Better reasoning is not a guarantee.

questions.stem: A coaching agent should recall what a user said in conversations weeks ago, for example "last month you mentioned a knee injury", by searching past sessions. Which ADK features fit? (Select two.)
options: A MemoryService (such as the Memory Bank-backed service) holding past sessions
The `temp:` state prefix
The `load_memory` tool so the agent can query that memory
A larger `output_key` value
questions.explanation: Memory is ADK's searchable, cross-session store, provided by a MemoryService and queried by the agent with `load_memory`. State is key-value data rather than searchable history, and `temp:` lasts only one invocation.
rationales: Correct.
`temp:` keys disappear after the current invocation.
Correct.
`output_key` stores one agent's final text. It is not a search mechanism.

questions.stem: An ADK app wraps Antigravity with `ManagedAgent` and also passes it a local Python function tool and an MCP toolset. The local tools are never used. Why?
options: The function needs a docstring
The `ManagedAgent` toolset is predefined on the server, so client-side and MCP tools are not supported
MCP tools only work with Deep Research
The agent needs `tool_choice="any"`
questions.explanation: ADK's `ManagedAgent` wraps a Google-managed agent through the Interactions API, and that agent's toolset is set on the server. To combine your own tools with model reasoning in ADK, use a regular `LlmAgent`, or configure tools on the managed agent through the Interactions API.
rationales: Docstrings shape a schema but do not explain this.
Correct.
Not the reason.
No tool choice can enable unsupported tools.

questions.stem: A 20,000-token policy document is sent with every question, but `usage.total_cached_tokens` is always 0. The prompt starts with the user question and a timestamp. What is the fix?
options: Switch to stateless mode
Put the stable document first and the variable question last
Create an explicit cache with `caches.create` on Gemini 4 Argon
Shorten the document below 4,096 tokens
questions.explanation: Implicit caching is automatic but only matches a shared prefix of at least 4,096 tokens on current models such as Argon and 3.8 Flash. Putting the question and timestamp first changes the prefix on every call, so put the stable document first and the variable part last.
rationales: Implicit caching works in both stateful and stateless mode; the mode is not the problem.
Correct: implicit caching matches prefixes, so stable content must come first.
Explicit caching is not supported on Gemini 4 Argon or the Interactions API.
Dropping below the minimum prefix length would make caching impossible.

questions.stem: Overnight extraction of 200,000 invoices must be as cheap as possible; results are needed by the next afternoon. What should you use?
options: Gemini 4 Argon at high thinking
Streaming responses
The Batch API, at 50% of standard pricing with a ~24-hour target
Synchronous calls at maximum concurrency
questions.explanation: The Batch API halves the cost for offline work, with results usually well within 24 hours.
rationales: Expensive for routine extraction.
Streaming improves perceived latency, not cost.
Correct.
Full price and rate-limit pressure.

questions.stem: A team creates four API keys in the same project to get four times the rate limit. What happens?
options: Limits quadruple
Keys are banned automatically
Each key gets free-tier limits only
Nothing changes; limits apply per project, not per key
questions.explanation: Rate limits are per project. To get more capacity, move up a tier or request an increase.
rationales: Limits are per project.
No such rule is documented.
Tier is a project property.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which errors should a Gemini client retry with exponential backoff and jitter? (Select two.)
options: 429 `rate_limit_exceeded` (per-minute limit)
503 `service_unavailable`
400 `invalid_request` from an over-complex schema
402 `payment_required`
questions.explanation: Per-minute rate limits and transient server errors clear on their own, so exponential backoff with jitter is right. A 400 needs the request fixed, and a 402 means prepaid credits are depleted, so retrying cannot succeed.
rationales: Correct: back off and retry.
Correct: transient, retry with backoff.
Deterministic: fix the request.
Credits are depleted; do not retry.

questions.stem: You need a 150,000-token output from Gemini 4 Argon. Which request setting is essential?
options: An explicit cache
`temperature: 0`
`store=False` to avoid storage limits
A `max_output_tokens` large enough for the output, since the default output cap is 65,536 tokens
questions.explanation: Argon supports long decode: `max_output_tokens` can be raised up to 1,048,576, but the default is 65,536, so without raising it the output stops early. Running it in background mode (which requires `store=True`) is the recommended pattern, and you join all `model_output` steps at the end.
rationales: Explicit caching is not supported on Argon and does not affect output length.
Sampling parameters are ignored on Argon.
`store=False` changes nothing about output length and blocks background mode.
Correct: long decode needs a raised `max_output_tokens`.

questions.stem: After a long-decode background interaction completes, the text looks incomplete. What did the code likely miss?
options: It used `previous_interaction_id`
It polled too slowly
It read only one `model_output` step instead of joining all of them
It forgot to set temperature
questions.explanation: Each long-decode hop in a background run adds a `model_output` step. Join the text of all of them to get the full answer.
rationales: Not the issue.
Polling speed does not drop text.
Correct.
Irrelevant.

questions.stem: Which change usually cuts Gemini cost the most for a routine workload?
options: Removing the system instruction
Streaming responses
Using more API keys
Moving from the flagship model to Flash or Flash-Lite after evals confirm quality
questions.explanation: Model tier is the biggest cost lever, followed by thinking level, output length and context size.
rationales: Saves few tokens and hurts quality.
Does not change price.
Does not change price or limits.
Correct.

questions.stem: A mobile app calls the Gemini API directly with an embedded API key. What is the main problem and fix?
options: The key can be extracted from the app; call Gemini from your backend instead
Mobile apps are not allowed to use Gemini
The key expires after 48 hours
Mobile networks cannot reach the API
questions.explanation: Never ship API keys to clients. Proxy calls through your backend, and keep keys in a secrets manager.
rationales: Correct.
They can, through a safe architecture.
API keys do not expire on a 48-hour clock (that is how long Files API uploads are kept).
They can.

questions.stem: Users complain a chat feels slow, though total generation time is acceptable. What helps most?
options: Use background mode for every chat turn
Stream the response so text appears as it is generated
Use the Batch API
Raise thinking_level
questions.explanation: Streaming reduces perceived latency in interactive UIs.
rationales: Adds polling delay.
Correct: improves perceived latency.
Increases latency.
Usually slower.

questions.stem: Which statements about implicit caching are correct (at the time of writing)? (Select two.)
options: You must call `caches.create` before every request
It requires `store=False`
It is on by default for Gemini 2.5 and newer models
Cache hits are reported in `usage.total_cached_tokens`
questions.explanation: Implicit caching is automatic and visible in usage; explicit caching is a separate, older mechanism.
rationales: That is explicit caching, which is a separate generateContent feature.
It works in both stateful and stateless modes.
Correct.
Correct.

questions.stem: Users upload contracts of wildly varying length. Before each call you want to reject inputs that would blow the per-request cost budget, and afterwards you want to log what was actually billed. What is the best approach?
options: Estimate cost from file size in bytes before the call and skip logging afterwards
Call `count_tokens` on the prepared input before sending, then log the `usage` fields from the response
Set `max_output_tokens` very low so input cost cannot exceed the budget
Send every request through the Batch API so cost is fixed per job
questions.explanation: `count_tokens` measures the actual prompt, including media, before you pay for it, and the `usage` fields (`total_input_tokens`, `total_output_tokens`, `total_thought_tokens`, `total_cached_tokens`) report what was billed. Byte size is a poor proxy, especially for PDFs and images.
rationales: Bytes do not map reliably to tokens, and skipping usage logging loses the real numbers.
Correct: measure before, read usage after.
Output limits do not cap input tokens, and a tight limit can truncate answers while thinking is still billed.
Batch halves the price but does not make cost per job fixed or enforce a budget.

questions.stem: An enrichment step runs inside an existing synchronous pipeline that cannot be refactored into file-based jobs. Results are needed within the hour, and cost matters more than latency. Which option fits best?
options: Priority tier, so requests are never shed
The Batch API with a JSONL file
The Flex service tier on the synchronous calls, with retries for shed requests
Standard tier with more API keys to raise throughput
questions.explanation: Flex keeps the synchronous call shape at about half price, in exchange for best-effort, sheddable capacity and latencies that can reach minutes. Batch would also be cheap but needs a job-based refactor and targets a 24-hour turnaround.
rationales: Priority costs more than Standard; it buys reliability, not savings.
Requires restructuring into jobs and has a 24-hour target, which risks the one-hour window.
Correct: cheaper, synchronous, acceptable latency.
Extra keys in one project add no capacity, and Standard is full price.

questions.stem: A free-tier prototype starts returning 429 `quota_exceeded` in the late afternoon and keeps failing even after a client backs off for several minutes. What is the right response?
options: Increase the backoff ceiling to 30 minutes and keep retrying
Create a second API key in the same project
Switch to streaming so requests count less
Treat it as a daily quota: wait for the reset at midnight Pacific, or move up a tier / request more quota
questions.explanation: `quota_exceeded` signals the daily limit, which resets at midnight Pacific, unlike `rate_limit_exceeded`, which clears within a minute. More capacity comes from a higher tier or a quota request, not from retries or extra keys.
rationales: Retries cannot succeed until the daily reset and waste effort.
Limits are per project, not per key.
Streaming does not change request counts.
Correct.

questions.stem: Overnight, every call from a prepaid account fails with HTTP 402 `payment_required`. The retry middleware has been retrying them with exponential backoff for hours. What should the client have done?
options: Failed fast without retrying and alerted the team that owns billing
Retried with a longer backoff and more jitter
Switched to the Flex tier automatically
Rotated the API key and retried
questions.explanation: A 402 `payment_required` means prepaid credits are depleted, so no amount of retrying will succeed. The docs say not to retry it; surface the error and get credits topped up.
rationales: Correct.
The condition is not transient.
Cheaper tiers still need credits.
Key rotation does not restore credits.

questions.stem: A mobile client streams long answers with `stream: true`. When users switch networks mid-answer the SSE connection drops, and the app currently re-sends the whole request, paying for the answer twice. What should it do instead?
options: Disable streaming so the request is atomic
Reconnect and resume the stream using `last_event_id`
Use `previous_interaction_id` to start a new turn that says "continue"
Lower `max_output_tokens` so answers finish before the network changes
questions.explanation: Streaming events carry ids, and you resume a dropped stream with `last_event_id` rather than generating the answer again. A new "continue" turn is a separate, billed generation that may not join cleanly.
rationales: Gives up perceived latency and long non-streamed calls are more exposed to connection timeouts.
Correct.
Creates a new generation and bills it again.
Truncates answers without fixing the reconnect.

questions.stem: A team wants Deep-Research-style runs to execute in the background but has a policy of `store=False` on every interaction. What happens if they set `background=True`?
options: It works; storage is only needed for streaming
The run executes but results are deleted after one poll
It does not work: background execution requires `store=True`, so they need a policy exception or a different design
The API silently switches to foreground mode
questions.explanation: Background execution returns an id and keeps the interaction server-side so you can poll or stream it, which requires `store=True`. The team has to allow storage for those runs.
rationales: Storage is required for background mode, not streaming.
Not documented behaviour.
Correct.
Not documented behaviour.

sources.title: Interactions API overview — Gemini API docs

questions.stem: A legacy service on `generateContent` with a Gemini 3.8 Flash model sends the same 80,000-token product manual with thousands of questions during business hours. Finance wants a guaranteed discount on the manual, not a probable one. What fits best?
options: Rely on implicit caching, since it guarantees savings above 4,096 tokens
Migrate to Gemini 4 Argon and create an explicit cache there
Use the Batch API for the live questions
Create an explicit cache with `caches.create`, reference it via `cached_content`, and set a TTL that matches business hours
questions.explanation: Explicit caching on generateContent guarantees the cached-token discount on supported models, and its TTL (default 1 hour) should match the reuse window because storage time is billed. Implicit caching is automatic but has no savings guarantee.
rationales: Implicit caching gives no savings guarantee.
Explicit caching is not supported on Gemini 4 Argon or later.
Batch has a 24-hour target and is wrong for live questions.
Correct.

questions.stem: A huge Batch API job submitted on Friday shows `JOB_STATE_EXPIRED` on Monday, and there are no results. What most likely happened, and what should change?
options: The job stayed pending or running past 48 hours and expired; split the work into smaller jobs and monitor them
The JSONL file was deleted after 48 hours; re-upload it every day
Batch jobs always expire on weekends; resubmit on Monday
The project hit its RPD limit; create a new API key
questions.explanation: A batch job that is still pending or running after 48 hours expires with no results. Smaller jobs, kept within per-tier enqueued-token limits, finish inside that window.
rationales: Correct.
The Files API retention is not what expires a job.
No such rule exists.
Extra keys add no capacity, and this is a job state, not a rate-limit error.

questions.stem: Hard prompts on Gemini 4 Argon often fail after about a minute with dropped connections, though the same prompts succeed in AI Studio. Which changes address this? (Select two.)
options: Raise the client timeout to at least 15 minutes
Run the work with `background=True` (and `store=True`) and poll or stream the result
Set `temperature: 0` to make reasoning faster
Spread the requests across several API keys
questions.explanation: Plain HTTP connections typically close after about 60 seconds, and Google recommends client timeouts of at least 15 minutes for Argon, or background execution for long work. Sampling parameters are ignored on Argon, and keys do not affect timeouts.
rationales: Correct.
Correct.
Sampling parameters are ignored on Argon.
Limits are per project and unrelated to timeouts.

questions.stem: A latency-critical fraud check must not have its requests shed during demand spikes, and the business will pay more for that. What fits best, and what happens if traffic exceeds the purchased capacity?
options: Flex tier; excess requests fail with 503
Priority tier; traffic above the priority limits gracefully downgrades to Standard
Batch API; excess requests queue for 24 hours
Priority tier; traffic above the limits is rejected with 402
questions.explanation: Priority (in preview at the time of writing) is non-sheddable at a premium price, and when you exceed priority limits it gracefully downgrades to Standard rather than failing. Flex is the cheap, sheddable option.
rationales: Flex is sheddable, the opposite of the requirement.
Correct.
Batch is for offline work.
402 means prepaid credits are depleted, not a capacity overflow.

questions.stem: An Argon workload costs far more than the team estimated. The estimate assumed visible answer lengths for output and cached-input pricing for a 30,000-token instruction prefix shared by every request. Which two `usage` readings best explain and target the gap? (Select two.)
options: A high `total_thought_tokens`, because thinking tokens are billed as output
A low `total_cached_tokens` on requests that share a long prefix, suggesting prompt ordering breaks implicit caching
A high `total_tokens` caused by streaming overhead
A non-zero `total_tool_use_tokens`, which proves the Batch API was used
questions.explanation: Output price includes thinking, so `total_thought_tokens` often explains spend above visible output; lowering thinking_level targets it. A low cached count on a shared prefix means you are paying full input price where implicit caching could have helped.
rationales: Correct.
Correct: reorder so stable content comes first.
Streaming does not add billed tokens.
Tool-use tokens relate to tools, not to Batch.

questions.stem: What is the default state of Gemini’s adjustable safety filters on Gemini 2.5 and newer models?
options: Block most content by default
Block medium and above for every category
They cannot be configured
Off; you set thresholds explicitly if needed
questions.explanation: Adjustable filters are off by default on 2.5+ models. Some core protections, such as for child safety, are always on.
rationales: Not for 2.5+.
Not the default.
They can, per category.
Correct.

questions.stem: How does a safety-filter block surface on the Interactions API?
options: An HTTP 400 error with no content and an error code such as `safety`
A normal response whose text says "blocked"
A 429 rate-limit error
A silent empty `output_text`
questions.explanation: Blocks return a 400 error (codes like `safety`, `jailbreak`, `prohibited_content`, `blocklist`). Handle them as a product state.
rationales: Correct.
The request fails instead.
Different error class.
It is an explicit error.

questions.stem: An email-triage agent reads incoming emails and can send replies. Which measures best reduce prompt-injection risk? (Select two.)
options: Raise thinking_level to high
Treat email content as data and require human confirmation before sending replies
Give the agent only the tools and permissions it needs
Set every safety filter to `block_low_and_above`
questions.explanation: Injection is mitigated by least privilege, treating untrusted content as data, and confirmation for consequential actions.
rationales: Does not prevent injection.
Correct.
Correct: least privilege.
Filters target harmful content, not injected instructions.

questions.stem: Gemini safety filters decide based on…
options: The user’s account age
The length of the prompt
The probability that content is unsafe
The severity of the harm
questions.explanation: Filters are probability-based, so a severe harm with low probability may pass a low-sensitivity setting. Add your own checks where needed.
rationales: Not a factor.
Not a factor.
Correct.
They use probability, not severity.

questions.scenario: A team launched a Gemini-powered tutoring app after tuning safety thresholds and passing an internal red-team review. Three months later, parents report the app sometimes gives age-inappropriate advice that the original tests never covered.
questions.stem: Which step of Google's recommended responsible-AI cycle did the team most clearly neglect?
options: Collecting user feedback and monitoring in production, then feeding findings back into risk analysis
Choosing a larger model with more parameters
Setting every category to `block_low_and_above` before launch
Removing the system instruction so the model behaves more neutrally
questions.explanation: Google's guidance describes an iterative cycle: understand risks, mitigate, safety-test, then collect feedback and monitor. The team treated safety as a one-time pre-launch step, so new failure modes went unnoticed. Monitoring and feeding feedback back into the cycle closes that gap.
rationales: Correct: the ongoing monitoring and feedback step was missing.
Model size does not replace monitoring and is not a step in the cycle.
Stricter thresholds alone would not have revealed new failure modes, and filters are probability-based, not a substitute for monitoring.
Removing guidance makes behavior less controlled, not safer.

questions.scenario: A legacy service still calls `generateContent`. Logs show some calls return a candidate with no usable text.
questions.stem: Which field tells the service that the model's response was blocked by safety filtering?
options: `promptFeedback.blockReason`
`Candidate.finishReason` equal to `SAFETY`, with `safetyRatings`
An HTTP 429 status code
`usageMetadata.totalTokenCount` equal to 0
questions.explanation: On the legacy API, a blocked response is reported with `finishReason: SAFETY` on the candidate, and `safetyRatings` shows the categories. `promptFeedback.blockReason` is for a blocked prompt, not a blocked response.
rationales: This reports a blocked prompt, not a blocked response.
Correct.
429 is a rate-limit error, unrelated to safety.
Token counts are not the signal for a safety block.

questions.scenario: A company is building a story-writing assistant for children on Gemini 3 using the Interactions API. The product manager says, "Gemini has safety filters, so we're covered."
questions.stem: Which responses to the product manager are accurate? (Select two.)
options: The adjustable filters are off by default on Gemini 2.5 and later, so the team must set thresholds explicitly
Filters measure the severity of harm, so anything severe will always be blocked
Developers remain responsible: add post-processing checks and run safety testing designed for children's use
Built-in protections cover every risk, so no further work is needed
questions.explanation: Adjustable filters are off by default on 2.5+ models, and Google's guidance puts the onus on developers to mitigate and test for their use case. Filters work on probability, not severity, and only a narrow set of built-in protections (such as child safety) is always on.
rationales: Correct: defaults are off on 2.5+.
Wrong: filters are probability-based, not severity-based.
Correct: the onus is on developers, with post-processing and use-case-specific testing.
Wrong: built-in protections are narrow and do not cover app-specific risks.

questions.scenario: An Interactions API client shows "Your message violates our safety policy" whenever a request fails with HTTP 400. Users complain the message appears for requests that look harmless, and logs show error codes such as `recitation` and `spii`.
questions.stem: What is the best fix?
options: Retry each failed request up to five times before showing the message
Set every safety category to `off` so the 400s stop
Branch on the error `code` and show code-specific handling, since not every generation block is a harm-category filter
Switch to streaming so blocks are returned as partial text
questions.explanation: Blocked requests on the Interactions API return HTTP 400 with an error `code`. Besides `safety`, there are other codes such as `recitation` and `spii` that call for different user messages and handling. Reading the code lets the app respond accurately instead of blaming the user for a policy violation.
rationales: Retrying the same input does not address the cause and wastes quota.
Thresholds don't control codes like `recitation` or `spii`, and turning filters off ignores your app's risks.
Correct: handle by error code.
Streaming surfaces a block as an `error` event, not partial blocked content.
